channel.title: Systemic Error
channel.description: Independent commentary by Paulo Santos on politics, power, technology, and the systems behind the headlines. This isn’t a glitch. It’s the design.

item.title: 'Massacre': Texts reveal Republicans panicking about midterms
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that three unnamed Republican strategists privately described an election night as a “blood bath” and a coming “massacre” for their party. Mark Halperin published the remarks on X, according to Mediaite, including one strategist’s assessment that Donald Trump had asked voters to behave as though he were on the ballot—and that they had done so.

Another strategist reportedly said Republican turnout assumptions were wrong. Halperin attributed the party’s apparent trouble to inflation, diesel prices, Iran, Israel, Epstein, data centers, Trump’s ballroom project, and Trump family business deals.

The reporting does not identify the strategists, reproduce their texts, specify which contests produced these reactions, or establish results for the 2026 midterms. Its central claim is therefore narrower than its headline: several anonymous Republican operatives appeared alarmed by an election night and interpreted it as evidence of serious midterm danger.

Power is not panic

Republican strategists worrying in private are not powerless spectators. Their party holds the institutional leverage described in the story: thin majorities in both chambers of Congress and a president capable of setting its political agenda. Their fear concerns losing power, not lacking it.

That distinction matters. Operatives may sound helpless when voters reject their assumptions, but those assumptions helped shape campaign strategy, governing priorities, and the decision to tie Republican candidates to Trump. If the party made him the organizing force of its politics, then poor results under that arrangement are not an inexplicable weather event.

Trump made the test personal

The most revealing reported remark is that Trump asked people to vote as though he were on the ballot. According to the strategist, they complied. That turns a supposedly local or congressional election into a referendum on the president by his own design.

Republicans cannot plausibly claim Trump’s political dominance when it mobilizes supporters and treat it as incidental when it repels voters. A party built around one man inherits his liabilities along with his base. The list Halperin supplied—from inflation and foreign policy to Epstein and Trump family deals—suggests accumulated political exposure, not a single messaging failure.

Anonymous dread is not evidence of a wave

AlterNet’s framing outruns what it presents. Three unnamed strategists expressing alarm can demonstrate elite anxiety; it cannot, by itself, establish a national “blue wave.” The article supplies no vote totals, district results, polling trend, turnout data, or methodological basis for projecting the 2026 midterms.

Even the timeline is inadequately explained. The piece invokes an election night as a forecast for future midterms without clearly identifying the elections being discussed. That missing context is not cosmetic. It prevents readers from judging whether the strategists were reacting to representative contests, unusual local races, or temporary results.

The weaker target is the voter

Political coverage often turns governing failure into a story about whether a leader can “rally the base.” That framing relocates responsibility from officials who wield power to voters whose loyalty is being measured. It treats the public as a turnout mechanism and politics as a branding problem.

The quoted cult expert offers a broader explanation centered on information control, fear, and demonization. That analysis may illuminate Trump’s movement, but it does not prove why any particular voter acted or why any particular contest turned. More importantly, psychological descriptions of followers should not eclipse the agency of Republican officials who chose to reinforce Trump’s authority because it served them.

The system behind the alarm

The larger pattern is a party discovering that personalist politics creates personalist accountability. Republican leaders accepted Trump as their central campaign asset, defended the structure built around him, and expected his coalition to preserve their congressional power. Private panic begins when that bargain appears less profitable.

But alarm among operatives is not institutional resistance, accountability, or reform. It is the sound of political professionals calculating whether the machinery they helped construct can still win. The consequential question is not how frightened they are. It is what those holding power did with it—and whether voters are beginning to impose a cost.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Photo of poll worker enraging MAGA is a hoax — and she's a Republican
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened The photo was real; the viral MAGA story attached to it was false. item.content:encoded:
What happened

The photo was real; the viral MAGA story attached to it was false. AlterNet, citing Mediaite and Rogers city officials, reported that a Minnesota election judge wore a commercially available Halloween costume featuring fake blood and the words “PROBLEM SOLVED.” Officials said she was not invoking Charlie Kirk’s assassination or making a political statement.

The unidentified woman told the city she would never support the message attributed to her. Rogers officials also disclosed, with her permission, that she was serving as a Republican election judge under Minnesota’s party-balance requirement. The city said the costume did not violate the state prohibition on party or campaign messaging, though officials would have asked her to cover it had the confusion become apparent.

Before that context emerged, Dustin Grage’s post surpassed 4.5 million views by Tuesday evening. James O’Keefe solicited reports from Minnesota election workers, Matt Walsh demanded federal charges and life-ruining punishment, and Eric Daugherty claimed the worker was mocking Kirk’s assassination and urged Republicans to keep voting.

The accusation outran the evidence

Calling the photograph itself a “hoax” is imprecise. AlterNet’s reporting does not establish that the image was fabricated or staged. The deception was the unsupported interpretation: prominent right-wing accounts converted an ambiguous Halloween costume into evidence that an election worker celebrated political murder.

Nothing reported indicates that these accounts first established the woman’s identity, intent, party affiliation or the costume’s origin. Yet uncertainty did not produce caution. It produced accusations, demands for arrest and warnings that hostile forces were seizing control.

That sequence matters. The outrage was not built from verified facts and then expressed too strongly. The most inflammatory conclusion arrived first; basic reporting followed later.

Who held the power

The election judge held limited administrative responsibility inside one polling place. The political influencers held the power to expose an unidentified worker to millions of people, define her intent without evidence and invite an audience to treat her as a criminal enemy.

Walsh went further than criticism. He called for federal charges, handcuffs and a decision that would “ruin her life.” O’Keefe used the image to solicit election-related tips. Daugherty folded the invented meaning into a broader claim that “these people” sought control of America.

The asymmetry is stark: one worker wore an ill-considered costume; nationally amplified figures supplied the alleged ideology, assassination reference and institutional conspiracy. Their reach transformed an ordinary lapse in judgment into a political prosecution conducted through social media.

The scapegoat was politically useful

The woman’s Republican affiliation destroys the partisan morality play, but it should not be treated merely as an amusing twist. The episode shows how little the target’s actual politics mattered. She was useful as a symbol of a supposedly murderous, election-controlling enemy until officials supplied facts that made the script untenable.

The misdirection runs downward. Instead of scrutinizing influential accounts that published severe allegations without adequate verification, the spectacle focused scrutiny on a relatively powerless poll worker. Her costume invited questions about judgment. It did not justify inventing her beliefs or demanding federal punishment.

Nor was this simply “confusion.” Confusion describes uncertainty. These posts displayed certainty unsupported by the reported facts.

Outrage as election propaganda

The larger pattern is the manufacture of institutional distrust from decontextualized fragments. A photograph from a polling place carries special propaganda value because it can be used to imply that election administration itself is partisan, menacing or corrupt.

That implication remained unsupported here. Rogers officials said the judge was a Republican serving within a statutory party-balance system, and they found that the shirt did not meet Minnesota’s definition of prohibited political messaging. Those details are not incidental; they reverse the power story sold to millions.

The consequence extends beyond one falsely characterized worker. When political media figures turn ambiguous images into proof of election malice, they make routine administration look like enemy occupation. The correction then has to compete with a narrative already engineered for anger, punishment and mass circulation.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump may be literally unable to comprehend that he lost: insider
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Trump biographer Michael Wolff believes Donald Trump may have resisted his 2020 election defeat because he could not comprehend the vote totals, rather than because he consciously intended to seize power. Wolff told journalist Joanna Coles that Trump struggles with numbers, received favorable information from aides, and came to believe his own false account of the result. item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Trump biographer Michael Wolff believes Donald Trump may have resisted his 2020 election defeat because he could not comprehend the vote totals, rather than because he consciously intended to seize power. Wolff told journalist Joanna Coles that Trump struggles with numbers, received favorable information from aides, and came to believe his own false account of the result.

The article also presents a competing interpretation. Psychologist Alan D. Blotcky told AlterNet that Trump was not psychotic and knew what he was doing, while psychiatrist Henry Abraham described erratic nighttime behavior without explaining Trump’s election conduct. None of these remarks clinically establishes why Trump acted as he did.

Incapacity does not erase agency

Wolff’s theory may address Trump’s private understanding. It does not resolve the political question: who exercised power, made demands, and tried to alter an election outcome?

The president of the United States was not a confused bystander receiving bad customer service. Trump held the country’s most powerful office. Even if he misunderstood vote totals, his inability or refusal to process defeat did not transfer responsibility to mathematics, psychology, or subordinates carrying “good news.”

The speculation trap

AlterNet builds the story around an arresting but unprovable proposition: Trump may have been literally unable to understand that he lost. That framing turns documented political conduct into amateur diagnosis.

Wolff’s personal observations can support an account of Trump’s habits. They cannot establish clinical incapacity. Blotcky offers the opposite interpretation, while Abraham’s remarks about nighttime behavior do little to settle the matter. The result is a carousel of psychological labels where an analysis of power should be.

The weaker actors become the explanation

Wolff says people around Trump understood the result but brought him favorable information. That identifies an enabling structure, not an excuse. Advisers near presidential power can flatter, comply, resist, resign, or disclose. Their choices matter.

But blaming courtiers alone also misdirects agency downward. A system organized around appeasing one officeholder exists because that officeholder rewards compliance and because institutions permit personal grievance to become government business. The powerful actor remains powerful even when his entourage helps insulate him from reality.

Intent is not the only measure

Whether Trump acted from calculation, self-deception, or some combination remains unresolved by the reporting. Political accountability does not require a definitive psychiatric explanation.

A president attempting to overturn a loss produces institutional consequences regardless of whether he privately recognizes the loss. Fixating on his inner state risks treating foreseeable harm as a medical mystery and replacing questions of responsibility with questions no journalist can conclusively answer from afar.

The system loves a personality puzzle

This is the larger pattern: political coverage often converts abuses of power into stories about temperament. The personality is vivid; the institutional machinery is harder. So readers get speculation about cognition while the offices, advisers, incentives, and failures that converted one man’s refusal into a national crisis recede from view.

Trump’s psychology may be unknowable from this evidence. The distribution of power is not. He held the presidency, others enabled him, and institutions had to absorb the consequences. That is the political story. Everything else is a compelling distraction.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: The day Trump woke America's sleeping giant
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet argues that Donald Trump and Republicans may have triggered a powerful electoral backlash among Hispanic and Black voters in the South. The article attributes the reported surge in turnout to high prices and low wages, but especially to anger over aggressive immigration enforcement and Supreme Court decisions weakening the Voting Rights Act. The piece was published on Election Day, before results were known. Its claims about Democratic gains in Texas and elsewhere—includin
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet argues that Donald Trump and Republicans may have triggered a powerful electoral backlash among Hispanic and Black voters in the South. The article attributes the reported surge in turnout to high prices and low wages, but especially to anger over aggressive immigration enforcement and Supreme Court decisions weakening the Voting Rights Act.

The piece was published on Election Day, before results were known. Its claims about Democratic gains in Texas and elsewhere—including a possible James Talarico victory and competitive statewide races—were predictions based on polling and early-vote figures, not established outcomes.

Political scientist Joshua Zingher told AlterNet that changing Southern demographics and voting rules could reorganize the parties’ electoral coalitions. He also cautioned that the long-term consequences remain uncertain and that Hispanic and Asian voters are likely to become more politically diverse over time.

Power did not disappear

The “sleeping giant” metaphor risks confusing electoral potential with institutional power. Black and Hispanic voters can punish officeholders, but they do not control ICE, federal enforcement policy, congressional procedure, or the Supreme Court. Republican officials exercised that power; vulnerable communities absorbed its consequences.

Nor did the Supreme Court merely introduce uncertainty. According to the article’s account, its Voting Rights Act rulings disrupted an electoral structure that had protected Black representation while leaving Republicans dominant statewide. The uncertainty concerns what follows—not who possessed the authority to rewrite the rules.

Backlash is not reform

The article is strongest when it refuses to reduce the election to inflation. Material hardship matters, but so do immigration raids, racial targeting, voting access, and the judiciary’s power over representation. Voters can react to several injuries at once.

Yet backlash alone repairs nothing. Even a large Democratic victory would not restore voting protections, constrain enforcement agencies, change the Court, admit new states, or produce accountability. Those outcomes require officeholders to make decisions after the ballots are counted.

Celebrating turnout without naming that responsibility turns people facing state power into inspirational scenery. They provide the votes; party leaders retain the discretion to decide whether those votes produce structural change.

The Democratic alibi

AlterNet identifies Joe Biden’s failure—or inability—to pursue major institutional reforms as part of the cycle. The distinction matters. “Couldn’t” describes a constraint; “didn’t” describes a choice. The article does not supply enough evidence to settle every disputed reform, but it correctly locates agency inside governing institutions rather than among voters who lacked the authority to act.

If Democrats gain power and again treat court reform, voting rights, statehood, or oversight as optional, they cannot plausibly blame public apathy. The constituency described here is already participating under rules shaped against it. Institutional caution by officials would be a decision, not a weather event.

The media watches the palace

The article also indicts political journalism for preferring elite intrigue to slower changes in participation, migration, and representation. That criticism lands. Palace stories arrive with recognizable protagonists and quotable feuds; structural disenfranchisement demands attention to rules, institutions, and people largely absent from elite newsrooms.

But demographic storytelling carries its own trap. Hispanic and Black voters are not fixed partisan assets, and Zingher explicitly warns against projecting a short-term backlash indefinitely. Treating racial groups as a Democratic reserve army replaces analysis with entitlement—and gives party leaders another excuse to avoid earning durable support.

The system behind the surge

The larger pattern is not that Trump accidentally awakened a demographic force. It is that officials used institutional power, courts altered the terms of representation, affected voters reportedly mobilized in response, and Democrats were handed an opportunity whose value depends on what they do with it.

Elections can expose a system’s pressure points. They do not automatically change the system. If energized voters deliver power and Democratic officials decline to use it, the failure will not belong to a sleeping electorate. It will belong to the people who were awake, in office, and unwilling to act.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump eating Cheesecake Factory tonight at the White House: report
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that the White House ordered Cheesecake Factory food for its midterm election watch party. White House digital strategy chief Kaelan Dorr posted a photo of a takeout bag, and a White House official confirmed the order to The Wall Street Journal. The order referenced Barack Obama’s campaign-trail joke that Donald Trump’s gold-heavy White House renovations looked as though “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Trump had answered the joke with insults, defende
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the White House ordered Cheesecake Factory food for its midterm election watch party. White House digital strategy chief Kaelan Dorr posted a photo of a takeout bag, and a White House official confirmed the order to The Wall Street Journal.

The order referenced Barack Obama’s campaign-trail joke that Donald Trump’s gold-heavy White House renovations looked as though “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Trump had answered the joke with insults, defended the restaurant as successful, and claimed the White House needed his renovations to become “clean, pristine, beautiful.”

AlterNet also cites commentary arguing that Trump and his allies inflated a joke about his taste into a culture-war dispute. The article does not establish what Trump personally ate that night—only that Cheesecake Factory food was ordered for the gathering.

The institution became a prop

The relevant power belongs to Trump and the officials operating the White House, not to Obama, columnists, or a restaurant chain. They control the building, its public presentation, and the government communications apparatus.

Using an official election-night gathering to answer a former president’s aesthetic insult turned the White House into scenery for one man’s grievance. Dorr’s post and the official confirmation helped convert that grievance into institutional messaging. The decision was trivial in material cost as presented here, but revealing in its use of public office: presidential staff treated mockery of Trump’s décor as something the White House itself should rebut.

The grievance machine

Obama’s joke supplied the provocation. Trump’s operation supplied the amplification. According to the reporting quoted by AlterNet, Trump raised the matter at multiple rallies, the official White House account posted about it, and allied media and political figures repeated the complaint for days.

That distinction matters. A joke has no governing authority. The president and his communications machinery do. Framing the episode mainly as an exchange of insults obscures who possessed the institutional capacity to make an aesthetic slight part of the national political agenda.

Populism by takeout bag

The defense of Cheesecake Factory also offered Trump’s allies a familiar pose: corporate consumption recast as solidarity with ordinary Americans. Amanda Marcotte, as quoted by AlterNet, described the episode as part of a pattern in which MAGA figures embrace mass-market products to portray Democrats as snobs.

The contradiction is already present in Trump’s own remarks. AlterNet notes that he warned supporters that $5,000 would buy little at Mar-a-Lago and called it unsuitable for anyone watching prices. The political performance therefore was not a rejection of elite exclusivity. It was an attempt to make elite power look culturally familiar by placing a recognizable takeout bag beside it.

Misdirection as political work

The weakest actors in this story are not the president or the White House staff but the public drafted into another manufactured argument about taste. The dispute invites people to choose between restaurant fandom and supposed liberal contempt while the officials with actual power escape scrutiny of how they use public institutions.

AlterNet’s framing participates in the spectacle even as it criticizes it. The food order is presented as political news because Trump’s communications operation successfully made it political news. The consequence is not that Cheesecake Factory gained or lost dignity. It is that presidential attention, staff labor, official accounts, and campaign rhetoric were organized around protecting the leader from ridicule.

Government by wounded image

This episode reveals a broader governing pattern: institutional power deployed to manage a politician’s personal image, then marketed as cultural representation. The grievance becomes content; the content becomes partisan identity; the partisan identity crowds out any question of public purpose.

The order itself was harmless theater. The political structure behind it was not harmless: a White House willing to spend its authority answering a décor joke is a White House teaching its staff and supporters that the leader’s vanity is an official concern.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump policies single-handedly crushing US tourism
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, citing Washington Post reporting, attributes a sharp decline in international tourism to policies under President Donald Trump. Federal figures reportedly showed year-over-year overseas visits falling 1.8 percent in June 2026, 7 percent in July, 11.8 percent in August and, provisionally, 4.3 percent in September—even as global tourism continued recovering from pandemic-era shutdowns. The reporting identifies two pressures: higher jet-fuel costs following Trump’s attacks o
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, citing Washington Post reporting, attributes a sharp decline in international tourism to policies under President Donald Trump. Federal figures reportedly showed year-over-year overseas visits falling 1.8 percent in June 2026, 7 percent in July, 11.8 percent in August and, provisionally, 4.3 percent in September—even as global tourism continued recovering from pandemic-era shutdowns.

The reporting identifies two pressures: higher jet-fuel costs following Trump’s attacks on Iran and increasingly intrusive border enforcement. The Post reported that Customs officers searched 55,000 international travelers’ devices in fiscal 2025, up 18 percent from the previous year, while visitors could be required to surrender passwords or risk denied entry and device seizure.

International visitors spent $176 billion in the United States in 2025, according to the World Travel and Tourism Council figure cited by the Post—a 4.6 percent annual decline. The evidence supports a substantial policy-driven drag on tourism, although the article does not establish that Trump’s policies alone caused every reported decrease.

Washington made the choices

Tourists did not collectively become irrational, and the industry did not simply encounter mysterious “headwinds.” The federal government chose the policies shaping the risk and cost of visiting.

The president holds the central institutional power described here: authority over foreign policy, immigration enforcement and executive-branch priorities. Customs officers conduct the searches, but the administration determines the enforcement regime that authorizes and rewards such scrutiny. Airlines, hotels and destination economies absorb consequences from decisions they did not control.

A border search is also an economic signal

A vacation depends on predictability. A traveler deciding where to spend thousands of dollars must consider not only airfare but whether an officer may inspect private messages, social-media accounts and work files at the border.

That prospect changes the product the United States is selling. The destination now comes bundled with possible digital exposure, confiscation or refusal of entry. Calling this merely “overzealous” enforcement understates the power relationship: government agents possess coercive authority, while foreign visitors can decline only by taking their money elsewhere.

The market cannot outrun the state

The administration’s economic posture, as presented here, is internally destructive. It celebrates commerce while imposing political costs that make commerce less attractive. The reported decline in visitor spending is not an abstraction: it means less revenue for airlines, hotels, restaurants, cultural institutions and workers whose livelihoods depend on international arrivals.

Businesses can advertise harder or cut prices, but they cannot reassure visitors that federal officers will not search their devices. Private industry is being asked to compensate for a deterrent created by public authority.

The framing still overreaches

AlterNet’s claim that Trump is “single-handedly” crushing tourism is sharper than the evidence supplied. The reporting presents falling visits, higher travel costs and expanding device searches, but it does not isolate the effect of each policy or exclude every other cause.

That exaggeration is unnecessary. The documented pattern is already damning: federal choices foreseeably made travel more expensive and entry more invasive while international spending declined. Precision assigns responsibility more effectively than a slogan that claims total causation without proving it.

The systemic error

This is what punitive government looks like when its costs escape the population initially targeted. An immigration crackdown advertised as control reaches tourists, employers and local economies because coercive systems do not remain neatly confined.

The larger pattern is an administration using institutional power to maximize suspicion at the border while treating the resulting economic damage as incidental. The weaker actors—the traveler subjected to a search and the business losing customers—are left to adjust. The officials who designed the conditions retain the power, and everyone downstream receives the bill.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Maddow cheers voters giving 'one-finger salute' to those saying no one votes
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened Rachel Maddow called South Carolina voters’ reported record turnout a “one-finger salute” to claims that voting is pointless or elections are rigged. AlterNet reported that turnout reached a 30-year high and that early voting also broke records, although the article did not provide official totals or identify the reports supporting those figures. Maddow argued that would-be authoritarians use fraud allegations and intimidation to discourage participation and discredit results. Lawr
item.content:encoded:
What happened

Rachel Maddow called South Carolina voters’ reported record turnout a “one-finger salute” to claims that voting is pointless or elections are rigged. AlterNet reported that turnout reached a 30-year high and that early voting also broke records, although the article did not provide official totals or identify the reports supporting those figures.

Maddow argued that would-be authoritarians use fraud allegations and intimidation to discourage participation and discredit results. Lawrence O’Donnell said relatives in South Carolina had described widespread anger. At that point, polls had just closed, and neither Maddow nor AlterNet reported a winner.

AlterNet described a close Senate contest between Darline Graham and Annie Andrews. It said Graham’s hesitant performance in an October 11 debate reinforced criticism that she was unqualified, while cited polls placed the race within their margins of error. Those names and several references in the report are unclear or internally inconsistent, so the article does not establish a reliable account of the candidates or final result.

Turnout is power, not a verdict

High participation matters because political power is exercised through institutions, not television catharsis. Voters choose officeholders; election administrators count ballots; legislatures write election rules; courts decide challenges. A surge at the polls can disrupt expectations, but turnout alone does not reveal what voters wanted or who ultimately gained authority.

Maddow’s celebration therefore outruns the evidence available at that moment. She acknowledged that she did not know the outcome. The turnout figures may rebut predictions of public apathy, but they cannot by themselves prove that voters rejected authoritarian politics, embraced a particular candidate, or shared one motive.

The machinery of demobilization

Maddow’s broader point identifies a real political mechanism within the story’s terms: allegations that every loss is fraudulent can do more than attack a single result. Repeated often enough, they teach supporters to accept only victories as legitimate and encourage opponents to see participation as futile.

The decisive actors are not vaguely defined “strongmen.” Candidates and political leaders make fraud claims. Parties amplify or tolerate them. Officials decide whether access to voting is expanded or restricted. Media organizations decide whether unsupported allegations are treated as evidence, strategy, or ambient controversy. Naming that chain of agency is more useful than treating democratic backsliding as a mysterious national mood.

AlterNet muddies its own case

The report wants turnout to carry a sweeping political meaning, yet it supplies little documentation for its central numerical claim. It also veers abruptly from commentary about Serbia and Brazil into a poorly explained South Carolina race, with references that do not form a coherent account.

That is not a cosmetic failure. Journalism about electoral legitimacy requires unusually exact reporting: official figures, identifiable candidates, clear dates, and a firm distinction between polling, results, and interpretation. Sloppy presentation gives readers emotion where verification should be and weakens the argument it is trying to advance.

Participation cannot substitute for accountability

The seductive version of this story is that voters showed up and delivered a cleansing rebuke. The harder truth is that participation does not automatically neutralize institutional attacks. A large electorate can still confront restrictive rules, organized disinformation, partisan administration, or post-election efforts to overturn results.

The systemic lesson is narrower and more durable: public participation can frustrate demobilization, but it cannot carry the entire burden of preserving representative government. The officials who control election law, certification, enforcement, and adjudication retain the greater institutional power. Turning turnout into a triumphant television moment risks obscuring where responsibility actually sits—and how much damage powerful actors can still inflict after the polls close.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: MLK Jr.’s only grandchild just made family history at the polls
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Yolanda Renee King, the 18-year-old granddaughter of Martin Luther King Jr., cast her first ballot, becoming the first of his grandchildren—and his only grandchild—to vote. King told CNN the experience was deeply meaningful after years of accompanying her parents, Martin Luther King III and Arndrea Waters King, to polling places. item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Yolanda Renee King, the 18-year-old granddaughter of Martin Luther King Jr., cast her first ballot, becoming the first of his grandchildren—and his only grandchild—to vote. King told CNN the experience was deeply meaningful after years of accompanying her parents, Martin Luther King III and Arndrea Waters King, to polling places.

King said her parents taught her from childhood that voting was a way to make her voice heard. The article does not identify the election, polling location, ballot she cast, or calendar date behind its use of “today,” leaving the event’s immediate political context unspecified.

Symbolism without a power struggle

King’s vote carries historical resonance, but she holds no institutional authority in this story. She is a young voter and activist exercising an existing right. The officials who determine registration rules, polling access, district boundaries, and election administration hold the relevant power, yet none appears in AlterNet’s account.

That absence turns politics into inheritance and inspiration. The article offers a family milestone while largely avoiding the institutions that decide whether voting is accessible, burdensome, or effectively obstructed.

The missing decision-makers

No government action caused the reported event beyond the ordinary age requirement that previously made King ineligible to vote. No official is accused of blocking her ballot, and the reporting establishes no new voting policy or dispute.

That matters because a sentimental narrative cannot support claims the evidence does not. The weakness is more basic: the piece invokes “voting rights” and “systemic inequality” without naming any law, administrator, or political decision. It gestures toward systems while declining to examine one.

A legacy made safe

Martin Luther King Jr.’s legacy is presented primarily as civic encouragement: participate, speak, imagine progress. That is the least disruptive version of a tradition rooted in organized pressure against institutions that denied Black Americans political power.

Yolanda Renee King’s own advocacy—on gun violence, inequality, homelessness, climate change, and voting rights—suggests a broader politics than the article develops. AlterNet reduces that record to evidence of continuity rather than asking what she advocates, which authorities she is challenging, or what resistance those demands encounter.

What the framing conceals

The headline promises family history, and the reporting delivers it. But the framing substitutes proximity to a famous name for political analysis. King becomes a symbol of democratic continuity; the machinery governing democratic participation disappears.

There is no demonstrated scapegoating of a weaker actor here. The misdirection is softer: attention moves from institutional power to individual virtue. Voting is treated as a personal rite rather than an act conducted inside rules written and enforced by identifiable authorities.

The systemic pattern

American political coverage often honors civil-rights history most comfortably when it can convert conflict into ceremony. A first ballot is meaningful. It is not, by itself, evidence that the struggle over political equality has been resolved—or even a description of where that struggle currently stands.

The larger pattern is journalism celebrating participation while leaving power unnamed. A democracy cannot be understood through voters’ sincerity alone. The consequential questions remain who writes the rules, who administers them, who benefits from them, and whose political agency those institutions expand or constrain.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Right-wing Newsmax is already licking their wounds
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reported that Newsmax guests reacted angrily as early Tuesday vote counts showed Democrats gaining ground and threatening Republican control of the House and Senate. Former White House political director Matt Schlapp claimed Democrats had “bamboozled” voters into blaming President Donald Trump’s policies for unresolved economic problems. Former senator Rick Santorum predicted Democrats would use congressional power to investigate or impeach Trump rather than address inflat
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reported that Newsmax guests reacted angrily as early Tuesday vote counts showed Democrats gaining ground and threatening Republican control of the House and Senate. Former White House political director Matt Schlapp claimed Democrats had “bamboozled” voters into blaming President Donald Trump’s policies for unresolved economic problems.

Former senator Rick Santorum predicted Democrats would use congressional power to investigate or impeach Trump rather than address inflation, grocery costs or gasoline prices. The article also cited election forecaster Charlie Cook predicting a severe Republican defeat, but it did not provide final results establishing which chambers or seats had changed hands.

Power was on the ballot

The central fact was not that television personalities felt wounded. Trump held the presidency, and Republicans entered the election with congressional power that Democrats were attempting to reduce or take away. Voters—not Newsmax, Biden or some unnamed socialist force—were deciding whether that arrangement would continue.

Schlapp conceded the durability of presidential power even while lamenting possible Republican losses: Trump would remain president for two more years. His reference to Senate voting rules also exposed the real concern beneath the complaints. Losing seats could constrain the administration’s legislative leverage, oversight protection and control over federal priorities.

Losing became deception

Schlapp’s explanation stripped voters of agency. If they supported Republicans, their judgment counted; if they rejected Republicans, they had been “bamboozled.” That is not analysis of an electorate. It is a permission structure for dismissing an unfavorable result without examining why people voted that way.

The maneuver also redirected responsibility toward Biden, who was not described as holding office in the article, while Trump was the sitting president whose party controlled Congress. Whatever responsibility Biden’s prior policies may bear for economic conditions, the reporting supplied no evidence establishing Schlapp’s claim that he “caused” the problem under debate. Institutional power belongs to current officeholders, and accountability follows power.

Santorum invented the alibi early

Santorum moved immediately from prospective defeat to prospective Democratic misconduct. Before the article established final control of Congress, he predicted investigations, impeachment and neglect of household costs. He also alleged that Biden-era policy deliberately increased prices, but AlterNet provided no evidence supporting that accusation.

This is preemptive blame allocation. If Democrats won, their victory supposedly reflected Trump’s usefulness as a political target rather than voter judgment about Republican governance. If economic problems persisted, Democrats would own those too—even though Trump would still control the executive branch. The argument assigns Democrats responsibility in advance while preserving Republican power from responsibility after the fact.

AlterNet blurred forecast and fact

AlterNet correctly exposed the grievance logic in the Newsmax remarks, but its own framing outran the evidence it presented. “Devastation” and a predicted “hell of a beating” are not final election results. Early tallies and an experienced forecaster’s judgment can indicate direction; they do not establish completed outcomes.

The article also declared that analysts showed Santorum was right that Democrats could thank Trump for victories and turnout. Yet the supplied text named only Cook’s prediction and did not present turnout data or analysis proving that causal claim. Mockery is not a substitute for precision, especially when the underlying story is about powerful actors trying to replace electoral accountability with narrative warfare.

The system protects power with stories

The larger pattern is familiar: officeholders exercise power, voters register consequences, and partisan media recast those consequences as fraud, manipulation or irrationality. The defeated side then treats public judgment as illegitimate while preparing to blame its opponents for governing constraints it still retains the power to impose.

That narrative does political work. It shields leaders from internal accountability, teaches audiences that adverse elections require no self-examination and turns ordinary democratic opposition into a plot against the country. The wound Newsmax displayed was not merely disappointment. It was the discovery that holding power does not guarantee protection from its consequences.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: South Carolina Senate seat flips to Democrat who defeated Darline Graham
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Democrat Annie Andrews won South Carolina’s 2026 U.S. Senate race against Republican Darline Graham, sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Peter Hamby called the race, Decision Desk confirmed that projection, and WIS10 reported that with 80 percent of votes counted, Graham had no remaining path to victory. Andrews, a pediatrician who had initially entered the race against Lindsey Graham before his death, prevailed despite South Carolina’s Republican lean and
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Democrat Annie Andrews won South Carolina’s 2026 U.S. Senate race against Republican Darline Graham, sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Peter Hamby called the race, Decision Desk confirmed that projection, and WIS10 reported that with 80 percent of votes counted, Graham had no remaining path to victory.

Andrews, a pediatrician who had initially entered the race against Lindsey Graham before his death, prevailed despite South Carolina’s Republican lean and an apparently stronger GOP showing in the governor’s race. The split result indicates that some voters supported Republicans elsewhere on the ballot but rejected Graham.

Graham emerged from a bruising late primary against Rep. Ralph Norman with Donald Trump’s support. Her campaign then faced sustained questions about her qualifications after she acknowledged little national-security expertise, redirected a discussion of Taiwan toward transgender athletes, and incorrectly said South Carolina had 50 million residents. Republicans ultimately spent $5 million defending a seat they had not expected to be competitive.

The power behind the candidacy

Darline Graham did not reach the general election through demonstrated command of the office she sought. According to AlterNet’s account, she reached it with a famous family name and Trump’s endorsement, which consolidated MAGA support after an ugly primary.

That is the central power structure: party elites and a national political leader helped convert proximity to a deceased senator into a credible claim on his seat. Voters retained the final authority, but Republican institutions determined which candidate would carry their banner—and then committed millions to rescuing that choice.

The Senate Leadership Fund’s $5 million “insurance policy” is especially revealing. The party recognized the danger clearly enough to spend heavily, yet its response was not to reconsider how Graham had been elevated. It was to purchase protection from the consequences.

Incompetence was not the whole story

Graham’s errors mattered because senators exercise power over war, trade, diplomacy, and federal spending. Saying national security was not her area of expertise while seeking a Senate seat was not merely an awkward debate moment. It exposed a gap between the authority she wanted and the preparation she brought.

Her pivot from the South China Sea to “boys in girls’ sports” showed the function of culture-war politics when substantive knowledge fails: change the subject to a familiar grievance. The reporting establishes the pivot, not its motive. But its political effect was plain. A question about geopolitical judgment became an opportunity to invoke a Republican social wedge.

Calling the campaign a collection of “gaffes” would therefore understate the problem. The issue was not verbal polish. It was whether partisan identity, inherited recognition, and presidential patronage could substitute for competence.

The voters rejected the substitution

The apparent ticket-splitting strips away the easiest partisan explanation. If the Republican candidate for governor performed better while Andrews won the Senate contest, at least some voters distinguished between party preference and the specific candidate placed before them.

Even Norman’s son announced that he was likely to vote Democratic for the first time rather than support Graham. That does not establish why the broader electorate voted as it did, but it demonstrates that opposition crossed an unusually intimate Republican boundary.

Andrews and Norman both attacked Graham as unqualified. That convergence mattered because it denied Graham the usual shelter of polarization. The criticism could not be dismissed simply as a Democratic line when her Republican primary opponent had made the same case.

A machine defeated by its own selection

The weak framing would be to present this result as an inexplicable Democratic upset or a personal collapse caused by debate-stage embarrassment. The stronger explanation in AlterNet’s reporting is institutional: Republican power brokers enabled a vulnerable nominee, Trump helped rally the base behind her, and national Republican money tried to contain the resulting damage.

South Carolina voters then imposed a consequence the party apparatus had attempted to prevent. The broader pattern is not that political machines always fail. It is that they routinely confuse their power to manufacture a nomination with the public’s obligation to ratify it.

Dynastic access opened the door. Patronage carried Graham through the primary. Money arrived when scrutiny exposed the candidate’s limitations. None of it guaranteed consent. That is the systemic error: institutions built to select capable public officials instead protecting their own choices—until voters make the cost impossible to hide.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: 'A drunk man waving a steak knife': Leaker unfurls new Trump prediction
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Miles Taylor, a former Department of Homeland Security chief of staff and first-term Trump administration critic, predicts President Donald Trump will react more aggressively to Republican midterm losses in 2026 than he did after Democrats gained 40 House seats in 2018. The article does not establish that a “blue wave” has occurred; it presents an Election Day forecast based on unspecified predictive metrics and Taylor’s expectations. Taylor says Trump respond
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Miles Taylor, a former Department of Homeland Security chief of staff and first-term Trump administration critic, predicts President Donald Trump will react more aggressively to Republican midterm losses in 2026 than he did after Democrats gained 40 House seats in 2018. The article does not establish that a “blue wave” has occurred; it presents an Election Day forecast based on unspecified predictive metrics and Taylor’s expectations.

Taylor says Trump responded to the 2018 defeat by privately raging about prospective investigations, publicly threatening a “war-like posture,” forcing out Attorney General Jeff Sessions, and overseeing the revocation of CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass. His “drunk man waving around his steak knife” remark described that 2018 press conference, not a new incident. Taylor now predicts Trump could contest close counts, pressure state officials, direct the Justice Department toward districts he calls stolen, and resist congressional investigations. Those are predictions, not reported events.

The power is presidential

The central political fact is not Trump’s temperament. It is his control of the executive branch. A president can remove senior officials, influence federal law-enforcement priorities, command public attention, and place subordinates throughout the government. Describing such a figure chiefly as “angry” or “unhinged” risks reducing institutional power to a personality disorder.

Taylor’s account of 2018 supplies the more useful evidence: Trump answered an electoral setback with an attorney general’s removal, threats toward an incoming congressional majority, and retaliation against a confrontational reporter’s access. Whatever one thinks of Taylor’s interpretation, those were exercises of presidential authority or actions taken by the White House—not merely embarrassing behavior at a press conference.

Loyalty changes the machinery

Taylor argues that two restraints from 2018 are now absent: advisers willing to refuse Trump and the incentive imposed by another presidential campaign. His first point matters most. Personnel determine whether extraordinary demands die in conversation or become government action.

If senior officials were selected primarily for loyalty, the danger Taylor describes would not come from one man becoming more furious. It would come from officials deciding that serving him requires using public institutions against electoral and congressional opponents. Taylor predicts pressure on state certification officials and Justice Department intervention in disputed districts. AlterNet provides no evidence that those steps have occurred, but the forecast identifies the relevant chain of agency: presidential demand, subordinate compliance, institutional consequence.

Prediction is not reporting

AlterNet weakens its own case by presenting a projected Democratic “blowout” with sweeping confidence while offering no named forecast, polling average, race analysis, or probability. “Most predictive metrics” is not a substitute for evidence. Neither is “blue wave” when votes and control of Congress have not been established in the supplied reporting.

That framing turns a serious account of possible executive abuse into political suspense. The article has firsthand testimony about Trump’s conduct after the 2018 election and a former official’s explicit forecast about 2026. It should distinguish those categories cleanly. Instead, it packages prediction as momentum and speculation as near-certainty.

The scapegoat script

Taylor’s predicted sequence is familiar in structure: reject an adverse result, portray ordinary counting or certification as theft, pressure weaker state actors, and enlist federal power in the accusation. The officials administering elections would then become targets for a conflict created from the top.

That is political misdirection with practical consequences. Attention shifts from the president’s refusal to accept institutional limits toward local officials forced to defend routine procedures. The supposed scandal becomes the count itself, while the actual power play—the attempt to make government validate an unsupported claim—recedes into the background.

A system built on voluntary restraint

The larger pattern is institutional dependence on officials choosing not to abuse the authority they possess. Taylor’s account suggests that advisers constrained Trump in 2018, at least intermittently. That is not a durable safeguard. It is an admission that formal power was being checked by personnel willing to risk saying no.

The decisive question is therefore not whether Trump will leave quietly, become angrier, or produce another grotesque spectacle. It is whether officeholders with concrete authority will obey improper demands, whether Congress can investigate without executive obstruction, and whether election officials can perform their legal duties without coercion. Political systems fail through decisions made by identifiable people. Temperament may generate the demand; compliant institutions deliver the consequence.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Under-the-radar Supreme Court petition could make Trump’s DOJ untouchable
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that disbarred lawyer John Eastman asked the Supreme Court to restore his California law license after disciplinary authorities found that he misled two courts while helping Donald Trump challenge the 2020 election. The court had not decided whether to hear his petition when the article was published. Eastman argues that officials punished protected political advocacy and compares his case with retaliation against civil-rights and human-rights lawyers. UCLA legal e
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that disbarred lawyer John Eastman asked the Supreme Court to restore his California law license after disciplinary authorities found that he misled two courts while helping Donald Trump challenge the 2020 election. The court had not decided whether to hear his petition when the article was published.

Eastman argues that officials punished protected political advocacy and compares his case with retaliation against civil-rights and human-rights lawyers. UCLA legal ethics professor Scott Cummings rejects those comparisons, arguing that Eastman was enabling government power and that his petition minimizes conduct the California bar treated as professional misconduct.

Cummings warns that a ruling for Eastman could also strengthen the Trump Justice Department’s campaign against independent attorney discipline. AlterNet cites a proposed DOJ rule allowing the attorney general to seek pauses in ethics investigations and a DOJ lawsuit intended to stop the D.C. Bar from disciplining former Justice Department official Jeffrey Clark.

The power is institutional

Eastman is the petitioner, but the Supreme Court holds the immediate power. It can decline the case, leaving California’s disciplinary judgment intact, or use it to redefine how far bar authorities may go when lawyers characterize professional conduct as political advocacy.

The larger power belongs to the Justice Department. State bars can investigate individual lawyers; the attorney general directs a federal institution with prosecutors, litigation authority and rulemaking capacity. Treating these forces as evenly matched would invert the hierarchy.

Politics is not professional immunity

Eastman’s argument, as described, attempts to move the dispute away from what disciplinary authorities found he did and toward the political identity of the person punished. That shift matters. If professional scrutiny becomes presumptively partisan whenever misconduct occurs during political advocacy, lawyers serving powerful officials acquire an escape hatch unavailable in ordinary practice.

The First Amendment concern raised by scholars supporting Eastman is legitimate but narrower than the immunity his argument could produce. Retaliatory discipline by partisan state bars would be dangerous. That does not establish that bar authorities must ignore findings that a lawyer misled courts. Political context cannot erase professional obligations without turning legal ethics into a privilege granted by proximity to power.

The civil-rights comparison reverses reality

Eastman’s comparisons to persecuted human-rights lawyers and NAACP attorneys do more than exaggerate his predicament. They recast a lawyer working to preserve presidential power after an election as the equivalent of lawyers confronting abusive state power.

That is the story’s central misdirection. The relevant distinction is not conservative versus liberal advocacy. It is whether disciplinary institutions punished political belief or responded to professional conduct within their jurisdiction. According to AlterNet, the California review department found the latter: Eastman misled two courts. His petition may contest that judgment, but historical analogy cannot substitute for rebutting it.

Accountability is being recoded as weaponization

The DOJ actions described by AlterNet reveal a broader strategy: label outside scrutiny “weaponization,” then use government power to disable the scrutinizing institution. The proposed rule would permit the attorney general to seek suspension of ethics investigations into department lawyers. The lawsuit against the D.C. Bar similarly places federal power behind an attempt to block discipline of Jeffrey Clark over his reported role in advancing Trump’s false election-fraud claims.

The article identifies the alignment but could state the power relationship more bluntly. Bar complaints may indeed be abused. Yet an administration does not cure that risk by giving its own leadership leverage to interrupt investigations of its lawyers. That arrangement makes the institution under scrutiny a participant in deciding whether scrutiny may proceed.

The system behind the petition

This case is not merely about whether Eastman practices law again. It tests whether lawyers acting for political leaders remain answerable to professional bodies outside the executive branch—and whether courts will preserve that external constraint.

The recurring pattern is institutional self-protection through rhetorical inversion. Powerful officials and their lawyers portray accountability mechanisms as partisan aggression, then invoke that alleged aggression to justify weakening the mechanisms. If that logic prevails, the consequence is larger than any single disciplinary case: legal ethics remain formally universal while becoming practically negotiable for lawyers backed by federal power.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump's admin fires a desperate Election Day salvage shot
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that the Trump Justice Department was preparing to send roughly 20 target letters in a criminal investigation involving the campaign of Alaska Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan. Citing NBC News and unnamed sources, it says the department had already issued 120 subpoenas. A target letter identifies someone as a focus of an investigation; it does not mean that person will be charged. The action followed a separate Justice Department lawsuit arguing that Sullivan’s pre
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump Justice Department was preparing to send roughly 20 target letters in a criminal investigation involving the campaign of Alaska Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan. Citing NBC News and unnamed sources, it says the department had already issued 120 subpoenas. A target letter identifies someone as a focus of an investigation; it does not mean that person will be charged.

The action followed a separate Justice Department lawsuit arguing that Sullivan’s presence on the ballot could confuse voters because Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan was also running. A court dismissed the administration’s attempt to block certification for lack of standing. The Alaska Supreme Court had already addressed the naming issue and prescribed how the candidates would be distinguished on the ballot.

AlterNet does not establish exactly when the target letters were sent, who received them, what suspected crimes underlie the investigation, or whether charges followed. It reports that the civil litigation continued separately and that the Justice Department filed a notice indicating an appeal, though legal commentator Chris Geidner questioned whether that notice was properly drafted.

The power sits with Justice

Dan J. Sullivan did not control federal prosecutors, subpoena authority, or the machinery that can place a criminal investigation over an election. The Justice Department did. According to the reporting, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Alaska and officials from the Civil Rights Division participated in the investigation.

That imbalance is the political core of the story. A candidate can defend himself in court and answer subpoenas. The executive branch can compel records, designate investigative targets, litigate over certification, and force everyone else to spend time and money responding. Even without charges, that power can reshape an election’s closing atmosphere.

Confusion was not the unresolved problem

The administration’s stated concern was ballot confusion between two men with similar names. But Alaska’s courts had already considered that problem and imposed rules for distinguishing them. The federal government nevertheless tried to turn the issue into grounds for blocking certification if the Republican lost.

That is not merely concern about clear ballot design. It is an attempt, as described by AlterNet, to make certification conditional on a preferred electoral outcome. The weaker actor—the candidate whose lawful ballot presence allegedly created confusion—became the focus, while the institution escalating a settled naming dispute wielded the real coercive power.

The article outruns some of its evidence

AlterNet calls the Justice Department “politicized” and presents the investigation as an Election Day salvage attempt. The sequence it reports supports serious scrutiny: extensive subpoenas, prospective target letters, certification litigation, and an election-related dispute already adjudicated by Alaska’s highest court.

But the article does not establish the letters’ precise timing or reveal the criminal evidence. Nor does it prove that every investigative step was ordered to rescue the Republican candidate. That motive is the article’s inference, not a demonstrated fact. The strongest indictment rests on documented institutional conduct: federal officials escalated an already-litigated ballot issue and sought leverage over certification.

Process can become punishment

The absence of charges does not make 120 subpoenas and approximately 20 target letters politically weightless. Investigations impose legal costs, generate damaging headlines, and allow insinuation to travel faster than adjudicated facts. When deployed around an election, prosecutorial process can create consequences before any court determines that a crime occurred.

The reported departure from the Justice Department’s traditional caution near elections matters for precisely that reason. Those norms exist because prosecutors possess powers that candidates cannot match and because an investigation’s public shadow can affect voters even when it produces no conviction—or no charge at all.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is executive power converting an electoral loss contingency into a legal controversy: if the favored candidate loses, challenge certification; if courts reject the theory, appeal; alongside that litigation, continue a broad criminal investigation carrying its own pressure and stigma.

Institutional abuse does not require polished lawyering or a successful courtroom result. It can operate through repeated escalation, forcing weaker actors to answer the government while officials present their own intervention as a response to disorder. Here, the reported disorder was two similar names. The consequential decision was the Justice Department’s choice to turn that manageable ballot issue into federal litigation and prosecutorial pressure.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump just woke up a force far bigger than himself
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that historian Heather Cox Richardson sees the midterm backlash surrounding Donald Trump as part of a larger revolt against concentrated wealth and government structured for a powerful minority. She argues that Trump did not create this political force but helped activate it by making exploitation under his second administration unusually visible. Richardson pointed to Trump’s unfocused appearance at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, private Republican fears of
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that historian Heather Cox Richardson sees the midterm backlash surrounding Donald Trump as part of a larger revolt against concentrated wealth and government structured for a powerful minority. She argues that Trump did not create this political force but helped activate it by making exploitation under his second administration unusually visible.

Richardson pointed to Trump’s unfocused appearance at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, private Republican fears of heavy losses, Elon Musk’s reported spending of at least $446 million on the midterms, and voters traveling long distances to cast ballots. She also noted that the Supreme Court rejected the administration’s emergency request to set aside roughly 20,000 California ballots.

But the outcome was not settled when Richardson wrote. Early voting and polling suggested a Democratic wave; only the completed count could establish whether one occurred.

Power is the point

Richardson’s argument is not fundamentally about Trump’s personality. It is about who controls government and who collects the rewards.

Presidents, congressional majorities, wealthy political patrons and the Supreme Court possess institutional power. Ordinary voters can remove elected officials, but only after navigating rules, money and administrative barriers largely shaped by people already holding power. A billionaire spending at least $446 million and citizens undertaking long journeys to vote are not equivalent forms of participation. One is concentrated influence; the other is the labor required to resist it.

Trump remains central because presidential power is real. His trade policies, the war with Iran, attacks on immigrants and governing priorities are not atmospheric disturbances. AlterNet says Richardson identified them, alongside corruption and ties to Vladimir Putin, as sources of his unpopularity. Republicans enabled that agenda through their control of governing institutions and their continued political dependence on him.

The convenient scapegoat

The unnamed Republican strategist’s reported remark—“We all know who the problem is”—captures the party’s preferred escape route. If electoral losses can be assigned to Trump alone, Republican officials can treat themselves as spectators to decisions they supported, excused or declined to stop.

That framing hides agency. Trump may dominate the party, but he does not enact an entire governing program by himself. Legislators vote. Donors finance. Operatives organize. Officials implement. Party leaders decide which conduct will carry consequences and which will be absorbed as the price of power.

Private blame after public obedience is not accountability. It is reputation management by people hoping voters will punish the figurehead while preserving the machinery around him.

Spectacle covers extraction

Trump’s reported speech offered a revealing contrast. Richardson described him spending roughly the first 16 minutes discussing the Reflecting Pool, blaming vandalism rather than poor workmanship, before turning to exaggerated claims and favored construction projects, including a golf course and a triumphal arch.

The spectacle matters because it consumes attention that might otherwise settle on material power. Arguments about a pool, monuments and presidential aesthetics are easier to stage than an accounting of whose wealth increased, whose rights narrowed and whose government was used for private advantage.

Richardson places that performance within a longer economic story beginning well before Trump. She cites tax cuts and deregulation since the Reagan era and an estimate that $50 trillion in income shifted toward the richest Americans over several decades beginning in 1975. Trump’s role, in her telling, is less architect than brazen exhibitor of an established arrangement.

History is not a guarantee

Richardson compares the present with earlier coalitions against enslaver power, robber barons and the concentration of wealth preceding the New Deal. The comparison identifies a recurring political conflict: elites accumulate economic and institutional control until a sufficiently broad coalition recognizes a common adversary.

But history does not operate like a pendulum with a preset return. Earlier reforms required organization, electoral victories and sustained use of government power. Public disgust alone produces nothing. Polls and early turnout can indicate movement without proving its scale, durability or cause.

AlterNet’s framing becomes weakest when possibility begins to sound like inevitability. Trump may have provoked opposition larger than himself, but the reporting had not yet established that this coalition would win, remain united or build the broadly responsive government Richardson anticipates.

The system survives its frontman

The larger pattern is not that one uniquely destructive politician periodically awakens the country. It is that concentrated wealth repeatedly finds political institutions willing to convert private advantage into public policy, while the officials involved insist the resulting hardship is accidental, technical or somebody else’s fault.

Trump’s conspicuous self-interest may make that structure easier to see. Removing him from the foreground would not remove the donors, lawmakers, courts, policies or incentives that sustained it.

The consequential question is therefore not whether voters reject one man. It is whether they identify the network of power behind him—and deny that network the opportunity to rebrand itself after using him.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Donald Trump is a radical hate preacher —and MAGA is his sick church
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet argues that President Donald Trump used racist and anti-Muslim attacks to mobilize supporters ahead of the midterm elections, casting him as a “hate preacher” and MAGA as a political congregation organized around personal loyalty. The essay points to his attacks on Somali Americans, Rep. Ilhan Omar, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and former President Barack Obama. According to the essay, Trump called Omar “garbage,” questioned her rights and citizenship, labeled
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet argues that President Donald Trump used racist and anti-Muslim attacks to mobilize supporters ahead of the midterm elections, casting him as a “hate preacher” and MAGA as a political congregation organized around personal loyalty. The essay points to his attacks on Somali Americans, Rep. Ilhan Omar, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and former President Barack Obama.

According to the essay, Trump called Omar “garbage,” questioned her rights and citizenship, labeled El-Sayed a “jihadist,” and invoked a “special metal detector” at an Iowa rally. It also says Trump answered Obama’s criticism of his White House renovations with insults and a stereotype about Black people and cleanliness.

AlterNet predicts major Republican losses and cites polls suggesting weakened support for Trump, including among white evangelical Christians. Those forecasts are not outcomes: the supplied text does not provide election results, a publication year, or enough methodological detail to evaluate every polling claim.

Power is not a pulpit metaphor

The church analogy describes Trump’s political culture, but it can obscure the more important fact: he is not merely preaching. In the account presented here, he holds the presidency, commands the executive branch, influences federal law enforcement and dominates his party.

That distinction matters. A demagogue with an audience can spread prejudice. A president who suggests sending federal forces to support a racialized “fight back” message can place state power behind that prejudice. The institutional danger lies in the combination of stigmatizing rhetoric, executive authority and Republican officials unwilling to impose limits.

The targets did not create the conflict

Somali Americans, Omar and El-Sayed do not control the presidency or the Republican Party. Yet Trump’s rhetoric makes them the objects around which political conflict is organized: immigrants become thieves, Muslim politicians become suspected extremists, and Black critics become people whose belonging or cleanliness can be questioned.

That is scapegoating, not policy analysis. It redirects attention from the officials exercising power toward minorities portrayed as alien, criminal or dangerous. The immediate political benefit is obvious even without claiming knowledge of Trump’s private motives: supporters are invited to treat vulnerable communities as the source of national disorder while the administration escapes scrutiny for its own decisions.

Republican agency cannot be baptized away

AlterNet’s fixation on Trump as preacher and MAGA voters as parishioners risks shrinking a governing coalition into a personality cult. Trump’s power depends on officials who can refuse him but instead validate, amplify or accommodate him. The essay names Vice President JD Vance and refers to congressional Republicans and governors as enablers, but gives Trump most of the analytical attention.

That imbalance matters. Party leaders possess votes, offices, budgets and procedural authority. When they repeat dehumanizing claims or decline to constrain the president, they are making political choices. “MAGA” is not a supernatural force that seized otherwise helpless institutions. Officeholders opened the doors.

Moral clarity needs evidentiary discipline

The essay is strongest when it identifies specific words, targets and offices. It is weaker when metaphor outruns proof. Calling Trump “fascist,” describing MAGA as a “sick church,” or predicting an electoral apocalypse may express the author’s judgment, but those labels do not substitute for demonstrating which powers were used, who enabled their use and what consequences followed.

The unsupported certainty is especially conspicuous in the election predictions. Polls measure opinion within defined samples and periods; they do not establish future results. A serious indictment of political conduct does not need prophecy. The documented rhetoric and the institutional authority behind it are damning enough to examine on their own terms.

The system behind the sermon

The larger pattern is rule through hierarchy: a powerful officeholder defines favored citizens as the nation and marks disfavored groups as suspect, while allied officials convert personal grievance into party messaging. The consequence is not confined to uglier campaigns. It makes citizenship conditional in political language and teaches supporters to see equal rights as privileges that leaders may revoke from designated enemies.

Trump is the central actor in AlterNet’s account, but the system is larger than one man’s appetite for adulation. It includes politicians who amplify him, institutions that accommodate him and coverage that can mistake spectacle for the machinery producing it. The sermon matters. The state power, party discipline and calculated scapegoating carrying it into public life matter more.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories
