item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that election-law expert Rick Hasen expects Republicans around President Donald Trump to keep “dancing around” his false claim that he won the 2020 election because they do not want to offend him. Despite the headline, the article supplies no clear prediction about when or whether Trump’s “big lie” will disappear.

Republican candidates and strategists reportedly see election denial as a liability in general elections, where voters are more focused on the economy. California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton has rejected Trump’s voter-fraud claims, while Senator Lisa Murkowski criticized a Justice Department lawsuit concerning an Alaska ballot issue involving two candidates named Dan Sullivan.

The retreat is selective. According to the reporting, some Republicans are distancing themselves publicly, some are staying quiet, and advisers are urging Trump to discuss more current issues. The party has not reached a principled reckoning; it is making an electoral calculation.

Power sets the boundary

Trump holds the institutional power identified in this story: the presidency, control over the MAGA base, and enough influence within the Republican Party that candidates and consultants fear contradicting him directly. Hasen’s description of advisers avoiding offense exposes the hierarchy. Trump establishes the permissible fiction; everyone else decides how delicately to evade it.

The officials and operatives around him still have agency. They can reject election denial plainly, as Hilton reportedly has, or challenge related government action, as Murkowski has. Those who remain silent are not trapped by confusion. They are choosing political safety within a system that rewards submission to the party’s dominant figure.

A tactical retreat is not accountability

The Republicans quoted here object mainly because the message is losing usefulness. Consultant Samuel Chen argues that economic conditions will drive more voters than “election integrity.” Consultant Christopher Nicholas says 2020 is old and that newer subjects are available.

That is not a repudiation of election denial on factual or democratic grounds. It is campaign triage. The concern is that the claim distracts from issues more likely to win votes—not that rejecting legitimate outcomes corrodes public trust and licenses future attacks on election administration.

The framing softens the conduct

AlterNet describes Trump as “flirting” with election denialism and Republicans as walking a “fine line.” Those phrases turn sustained false claims and calculated avoidance into awkward social behavior. The relevant actors are not struggling to understand what happened in 2020. According to the article, they are deciding how much truth they can state without angering Trump.

The headline also oversells Hasen’s remark as a bold prediction. What the reporting actually establishes is narrower: Republicans are trying to move away from an electorally damaging message while avoiding a direct confrontation with the man who continues promoting it.

The lie remains available

A message abandoned because it polls badly has not been discredited inside the institution that amplified it. It has merely been shelved. If Republican leaders refuse to say clearly that Trump lost in 2020, they preserve the underlying permission structure: election results may be treated as legitimate when convenient and suspect when defeat requires an explanation.

That is the larger pattern. Party elites tolerate propaganda while it mobilizes supporters, then quietly change subjects when it becomes costly. Their restraint is not powerlessness. It is an exercise of agency designed to preserve access to power without accepting responsibility for how that power was built.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Frank Luntz: Trump’s GOP made 'cardinal mistake of politics'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened Frank Luntz said Republicans made the “cardinal mistake of politics” by promising voters results and failing to deliver. AlterNet reported that, during a CNN appearance on Election Day, the Republican pollster described a panel of 2024 Trump voters who planned to support Democrats in the midterms, chiefly because of broken promises and the affordability crisis. Most panelists were voting against Republicans rather than expressing firm support for Democrats. One said the country had
item.content:encoded:
What happened

Frank Luntz said Republicans made the “cardinal mistake of politics” by promising voters results and failing to deliver. AlterNet reported that, during a CNN appearance on Election Day, the Republican pollster described a panel of 2024 Trump voters who planned to support Democrats in the midterms, chiefly because of broken promises and the affordability crisis.

Most panelists were voting against Republicans rather than expressing firm support for Democrats. One said the country had declined sharply over two years and that Democrats deserved another chance. Luntz also warned that political leaders might answer Republican losses with revenge instead of solutions, though the report offered no evidence that Trump or anyone else had decided to do so.

At the time of the report, polling suggested Republicans could lose the House, possibly the Senate, and key governorships. The article did not provide election results. Luntz urged Democrats, if they won, to address affordability and quality of life rather than begin with impeachment.

Power produced the backlash

These voters did not abandon the party because it lacked influence. They turned against it after Republicans held enough institutional power to be judged on results. Trump and the Republican Party made the commitments; people living with high costs assessed the delivery.

That distinction matters. “Distrust” did not simply descend upon American politics. Luntz’s panel described a recognizable chain of responsibility: officials sought power with promises, exercised power, and failed to produce the outcomes some of their own voters expected. The electorate’s response was not mysterious alienation. It was judgment.

Accountability becomes “partisanship”

Luntz’s advice to Democrats collapses two separate obligations into one convenient warning. Improving daily life and investigating official misconduct are not mutually exclusive. Calling impeachment inherently “political” evades the relevant question: whether conduct warrants constitutional scrutiny.

This framing protects powerful actors by making accountability sound like emotional retaliation. Republicans may be punished at the ballot box for governing failures, yet Democrats are instructed to treat any further examination of those failures as proof that they are equally partisan. That is not neutrality. It is an asymmetrical demand for restraint from the party that may inherit power.

The weaker actors are not the cause

The story gestures toward a public that believes neither the media, Congress, nor the Supreme Court. But generalized distrust can blur responsibility. Institutions do not lose legitimacy through some spontaneous defect in the population; their conduct, leadership, and incentives shape whether people consider them credible.

The panelists were not fickle consumers disappointed by branding. They were voters responding to material conditions and perceived broken commitments. Describing the result mainly as a crisis of belief risks shifting attention from officeholders who controlled policy to citizens who stopped trusting them.

A warning without evidence

Luntz said he feared Washington figures might use electoral losses as an excuse to “get even” or “seek revenge.” AlterNet sharpened that concern into a warning that Trump may seek revenge, but the reporting supplied no stated plan, decision, or action establishing that outcome.

The concern may be politically significant, but it remains Luntz’s forecast. A responsible analysis should not convert apprehension into fact—especially when the article’s stronger evidence concerns something more concrete: former Trump voters blamed Republicans for unmet promises and worsening affordability.

The governing bargain is breaking

The larger pattern is a political class eager to convert material failure into a story about tone. Voters name costs, quality of life, and promises that went unfulfilled; elite commentary answers with abstractions about trust, revenge, and excessive partisanship.

That maneuver narrows the consequences of governing failure. Republicans are permitted to seek and wield power, but their opponents are warned that accountability could look uncivil. Democrats, meanwhile, are offered a false choice between improving lives and examining abuses. The system’s recurring error is not simply overpromising. It is treating the exercise of power as legitimate while portraying serious consequences for those who exercised it as dangerously political.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Fox News 'caught off-guard' by Trump’s 'shocking' last-minute Hail Mary
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used an Election Day call to Fox & Friends to announce that the United States would end $4 billion in aid to Israel after the end of the year. Trump said he had reached the agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “months ago.” Fox News hosts Bret Baier and Stuart Varney said the unsolicited announcement shocked them and questioned whether it was intended to influence midterm voters. The report supplies no confirmation fr
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used an Election Day call to Fox & Friends to announce that the United States would end $4 billion in aid to Israel after the end of the year. Trump said he had reached the agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “months ago.” Fox News hosts Bret Baier and Stuart Varney said the unsolicited announcement shocked them and questioned whether it was intended to influence midterm voters.

The report supplies no confirmation from Netanyahu, the administration, or any documentary record that such an agreement existed. It says the arrangement had not previously been discussed publicly. Baier connected the timing to campaigns where Israel funding had become an issue, including Michigan, but neither host established Trump’s reason.

AlterNet also reports severe political headwinds for Republicans: a poll put Trump’s approval at 32 percent, gave Democrats an eight-point generic-ballot lead, and found that 50 percent of independents viewed their congressional vote as a vote against Trump. Baier said inflation, negative economic sentiment, and the Iran war would weigh heavily on voters, while warning that Republicans could lose their Senate majority.

The power was in the announcement

Trump was not a bystander floating an opinion. According to the report, he was the president announcing a major reversal of American policy and attributing it to a private agreement with a foreign leader. That institutional position gave an unsupported claim immediate political force.

Fox’s hosts possessed media power, but not executive power. Their surprise is therefore secondary. The consequential act was Trump’s decision to announce the purported deal without prior public explanation, supporting evidence, or an identified policy process.

Surprise is not scrutiny

The article’s “caught off-guard” framing turns attention toward the hosts’ reaction when the more important question is whether the president’s claim was true and operationally meaningful. AlterNet does not establish either point.

Baier and Varney wondered aloud about Trump’s motive and the electoral timing. That is reasonable speculation, clearly presented as such. But surprise is not accountability. A network that provides the president a live platform cannot substitute its presenters’ astonishment for verification of a claim involving billions of dollars and a major ally.

The Hail Mary remains an inference

The electoral context makes tactical intent plausible: Trump made the announcement on Election Day, Israel funding was reportedly salient in some races, and his approval numbers were dismal. Varney explicitly asked whether Trump was trying to affect the vote.

But the reporting does not prove that motive. Calling the statement a desperate electoral maneuver goes beyond the established facts. What can be said is narrower and more damaging: Trump injected an unverified foreign-policy announcement into the final hours of voting, and Fox broadcast it before its own prominent hosts could explain why it had happened.

A referendum he claimed

Baier said Trump had encouraged voters to act as though his name were on the ballot. That matters because it assigns agency where it belongs. If Republican candidates suffered from public anger over prices, war, or the administration’s performance, weaker actors did not manufacture that liability. Trump deliberately attached himself to the election.

The polling cited by AlterNet does not predict the result or prove why any voter chose a candidate. It does show the scale of the exposure: independents were far more likely to describe their vote as opposition to Trump than support for him, while voters preferred Democrats on the cost of living by 43 percent to 32 percent.

Government by last-minute spectacle

The larger pattern is executive politics conducted as media interruption. A president announces an enormous policy change on friendly television; the network treats its own confusion as the story; motive speculation outruns verification; and voters are left to sort policy from campaign theater in real time.

That structure rewards the official who can create the disruption. The claim dominates attention whether it is implemented, abandoned, clarified, or denied later. Institutional power produces the spectacle, media power amplifies it, and the absence of evidence becomes another segment of television suspense.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Another 'Mitch McConnell situation' underway as GOP rep goes MIA
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reported that 84-year-old Republican Rep. John Carter of Texas had largely disappeared from the campaign trail, appearing for some votes in mid-September but seldom in public for months. Carter attributed his absence only to “issues at home” and said he remained capable of serving. Former Georgetown Mayor Dale Ross told reporter Jake Lahut that he had heard Carter was experiencing serious memory loss and other possible illnesses. Those claims were not confirmed by Carter o
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reported that 84-year-old Republican Rep. John Carter of Texas had largely disappeared from the campaign trail, appearing for some votes in mid-September but seldom in public for months. Carter attributed his absence only to “issues at home” and said he remained capable of serving.

Former Georgetown Mayor Dale Ross told reporter Jake Lahut that he had heard Carter was experiencing serious memory loss and other possible illnesses. Those claims were not confirmed by Carter or established through medical evidence. Lahut said he decided to publish after Austin NPR affiliate KUT aired a brief interview in which Carter’s speech appeared difficult to understand.

Carter did not attend an event outside his campaign office where Democratic opponent Justin Early and supporters asked where he was. The reporting did not establish Carter’s medical condition or precisely why he had remained out of public view.

The office is not personal property

Carter holds the institutional power. He occupies a congressional seat, casts federal votes and benefits from the authority, staff and political infrastructure attached to incumbency. His opponent and constituents can ask questions, stage events and vote. They cannot compel a candid account of whether Carter remains able to perform the job.

Ross’s explanation cuts to the entitlement underneath the mystery: Carter “just likes being a congressman.” That is an observation from a former Republican official, not proof of Carter’s motives. But the surrounding structure is plain. Long tenure can turn public office into something an incumbent and his circle treat as theirs to retain until defeat, resignation or death forces the issue.

The gatekeepers made the absence possible

Carter alone did not create the information vacuum. Staff and party allies possess the access needed to clarify his schedule, explain his prolonged absence or provide credible evidence that he is actively performing his duties. According to the reporting presented here, the public received only a vague reference to problems at home and an assertion that he was well enough to serve.

That response protects the officeholder while transferring uncertainty to everyone else. Constituents are left to interpret scattered votes, an unclear phone interview and secondhand claims about his health. The people controlling access keep control; the public gets speculation.

Age is the hook, accountability is the issue

The comparison to Mitch McConnell encourages a familiar discussion about elderly politicians. Age matters when health may affect official capacity, but age alone proves nothing. The relevant question is whether an officeholder can perform public duties and whether those shielding him will provide enough evidence for voters to judge.

Reducing the story to another gerontocracy spectacle lets the party machinery escape scrutiny. The scandal is not that an 84-year-old might become ill. It is that an incumbent can become largely unavailable while the institution around him supplies no adequate public accounting.

Uncertainty serves the powerful

The weakest framing would make this a quirky disappearance story: supporters chant, an opponent brings coffee and doughnuts, and reporters hunt for an elusive congressman. That theater risks misdirecting attention toward campaign antagonists or rumor rather than toward the people with the power to answer basic questions.

Lahut was right to acknowledge suspicion about late campaign tips. Ross’s account remains hearsay, and an unclear interview is not a diagnosis. But uncertainty does not require journalistic paralysis. It requires precise reporting about what can be established: Carter was reportedly absent, his explanation was limited, and neither he nor his operation supplied a clear account resolving legitimate questions about his capacity and activity.

Incumbency thrives behind closed doors

This episode exposes a broader failure of American political institutions: they rely heavily on officeholders and their loyalists to disclose incapacity that may threaten their own control. The incentive is obvious. A candid admission can weaken an incumbent, end a career or cost a party a seat. Silence preserves every option for those already holding power.

The consequence is government by gatekeepers. Staff, allies and party officials can maintain the appearance of continuity while voters are denied the information needed to evaluate who is actually exercising authority. The systemic error is not human aging. It is a political order that treats transparency about an officeholder’s capacity as optional whenever disclosure might inconvenience the people protecting the seat.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump has reached his expiration date — and favorite excuse no longer works
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Donald Trump’s familiar defense—claiming credit for favorable developments while blaming Joe Biden for economic pain—had lost much of its political force before the November 3, 2026 midterms. Although Biden had left office 21 months earlier, a Reuters review found that Trump mentioned him nearly 900 times over nine months, frequently while discussing prices and affordability. The article says voters increasingly held the sitting president responsible. Polls ci
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump’s familiar defense—claiming credit for favorable developments while blaming Joe Biden for economic pain—had lost much of its political force before the November 3, 2026 midterms. Although Biden had left office 21 months earlier, a Reuters review found that Trump mentioned him nearly 900 times over nine months, frequently while discussing prices and affordability.

The article says voters increasingly held the sitting president responsible. Polls cited by AlterNet placed Trump’s economic approval mostly in the low 30s, while a late-September Reuters/Ipsos poll put it at 17 percent. The same reporting linked his political decline to public dissatisfaction with tariffs, immigration policy and the conflict with Iran, though the precise economic effect of the fluctuating tariff regime remained uncertain.

Republican candidates in vulnerable states were therefore confronting an election shaped by Trump’s record, not Biden’s. The article was written before the reported election result was available, so it establishes the political conditions surrounding the vote, not its outcome.

The power belongs to the incumbent

Trump was not a commentator diagnosing somebody else’s economy. He controlled the executive branch. His administration chose to expand tariffs, intensify immigration restrictions and enter a conflict with Iran after he had campaigned on stopping wars.

That institutional power makes the Biden refrain less an explanation than an attempt to detach authority from accountability. A president can reasonably argue that inherited conditions constrain policy. But after 21 months, repeatedly invoking a predecessor cannot erase who now signs executive orders, directs foreign policy and sets the administration’s economic agenda.

The decisions have names

The tariff expansion did not arrive as an atmospheric disturbance. Trump announced a new regime through an April 2025 executive order and branded the occasion “Liberation Day.” AlterNet appropriately notes that the shifting rates, reversals and suspensions make the policy’s exact effects difficult to isolate. What is not difficult to identify is who imposed the policy and who possessed the power to alter it.

The same distinction applies to Iran. Trump had explicitly promised that he would stop wars rather than start one. Seven months of conflict did not prove every voter’s theory about fuel prices, but it exposed a direct contradiction between campaign positioning and presidential conduct. Pew’s finding that 73 percent of Americans were highly concerned about higher fuel costs shows the consequence Republicans faced: foreign policy was being judged through household budgets.

Blame is not an economic program

The article’s strongest evidence is not that every price increase can be traced neatly to one Trump policy. It cannot. Its stronger point is political: voters no longer accepted Biden as the default answer to every unfavorable condition.

That shift matters because Trump’s 2024 campaign depended on making the incumbent own economic dissatisfaction. Once restored to office, he tried to preserve the same allocation of blame while reversing its direction of accountability. The argument was structurally absurd: presidential power was supposedly decisive when conditions improved, yet irrelevant when voters disliked the results.

Republicans cannot separate themselves

Trump reportedly urged voters at battleground-state rallies to imagine that he was on the ballot. For vulnerable Republican candidates, that invitation converted congressional races into judgments on an unpopular president whose economic record they had little appetite to defend. Their reluctance to discuss tariffs was itself revealing. A governing party confident in its signature policy does not treat that policy as hazardous material.

The cited generic-ballot advantage for Democrats and the large share of voters describing their vote as opposition to Trump did not guarantee an electoral result. Polls measure opinion at a particular moment; they do not count future ballots. But they showed the governing coalition losing control of the argument on the issue that had helped return it to power.

Accountability eventually changes address

This story reveals a recurring political pattern: leaders exploit public anger at incumbents, then resist the same standard once they inherit the office. Trump’s problem was not simply that an excuse had grown old. It was that his presidency had accumulated decisions, consequences and contradictions that a predecessor’s name could no longer obscure.

Political messaging can delay responsibility, but it cannot permanently relocate power. The person occupying the presidency commands the government and receives the judgment attached to it. Trump asked voters to treat the midterms as a referendum on him. According to the evidence AlterNet assembled before the vote, many were prepared to do exactly that.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump chief squirms as affordability brag unravels on camera
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent claimed in an ABC13 interview that food costs had “dropped substantially,” then immediately corrected himself: the rate at which food costs are increasing had dropped. As AlterNet notes, ABC13 clarified the essential point—food prices were still rising, just more slowly. Bessent acknowledged that conditions remained short of the Trump administration’s goals. He attributed some hardship to the war with Iran and the resulting energy-price spike, while
item.content:encoded:
What happened

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent claimed in an ABC13 interview that food costs had “dropped substantially,” then immediately corrected himself: the rate at which food costs are increasing had dropped. As AlterNet notes, ABC13 clarified the essential point—food prices were still rising, just more slowly.

Bessent acknowledged that conditions remained short of the Trump administration’s goals. He attributed some hardship to the war with Iran and the resulting energy-price spike, while pointing to lower egg prices and unemployment, claimed real-wage growth of 1 percent since Trump took office, and declining core inflation in three of the previous four months. ABC13 also reported that gasoline cost roughly a dollar more than a year earlier and interest rates were higher.

The interview aired as voters prepared for Tuesday’s midterm elections, though the report does not provide a calendar date. With affordability shaping votes in Texas and some polls giving Democrats a narrow advantage on the economy, Bessent offered the prospect of relief after hostilities ended rather than evidence that household costs had already fallen.

The correction contains the story

Prices and inflation are not interchangeable. Slower inflation means prices continue rising at a reduced pace; it does not restore what households have lost to previous increases. Bessent’s first formulation converted a deceleration into a decline, producing a more favorable claim than the facts described by ABC13 supported.

That distinction is not academic at the grocery register. Administration officials can celebrate an improving rate while families still pay more in absolute dollars. The correction exposed the distance between the metric being advertised and the condition voters actually experience.

Power owns the result

Bessent is not a detached commentator. As Treasury secretary, he speaks for an administration that holds executive power and asks voters to credit it for favorable indicators. That same administration must therefore answer for the conditions under which its economic claims are made.

The reporting does not establish that every price increase resulted from a White House decision. It does establish a political asymmetry: officials claim agency when wages, employment, or core inflation improve, then shift attention to war and energy markets when living costs remain painful. External forces may be real, but they cannot serve as an all-purpose exemption from accountability.

A promise substituted for relief

Bessent’s case depended partly on anticipated improvement: oil markets would be better supplied after hostilities, and a prospective deal with Iran had helped oil prices fall 7 percent that day. Those developments may support optimism. They do not prove durable relief for households, and the report does not say that the prospective agreement was completed.

This is the administration’s weaker political offer: endure current costs and trust that postwar conditions will eventually repair them. The official with institutional authority presented a forecast; voters were left with the bill.

The framing softens responsibility

AlterNet’s language about Bessent being “forced” into an “embarrassing correction” personalizes the episode as an on-camera stumble. The more consequential issue is not discomfort. It is the use of statistical language to make continuing price increases sound like falling costs.

Calling the moment a squirm risks turning economic messaging into theater. The institutional act was simpler and more serious: a senior official made an inaccurate boast, corrected it only within the same sentence, and continued selling partial indicators as evidence of recovery. ABC13’s clarification supplied the accountability the claim itself lacked.

The systemic error

Modern economic messaging routinely asks the public to judge power through rates of change while living with accumulated prices, debt costs, rent, health expenses, and wages. That gap is politically useful because officials can identify a favorable trend without demonstrating that ordinary people are materially better off.

The larger pattern is selective ownership. Governments present improvement as the product of leadership and hardship as the product of circumstance. Bessent’s correction briefly stripped away that arrangement: food costs had not substantially dropped. The administration had a better statistic, a future promise, and an election arriving before either became cheaper groceries.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Psychologist exposes Trump falling asleep standing up in disaster speech
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump appeared to drift off while standing during Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s remarks at a Monday event near the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Psychologist John Paul Garrison reviewed footage and said he believed Trump briefly fell asleep, appeared “barely conscious” while attempting to applaud, and displayed spasms. The event was presented as Trump’s closing midterm message, but AlterNet says he spent at least ten minutes discussing
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump appeared to drift off while standing during Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s remarks at a Monday event near the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Psychologist John Paul Garrison reviewed footage and said he believed Trump briefly fell asleep, appeared “barely conscious” while attempting to applaud, and displayed spasms.

The event was presented as Trump’s closing midterm message, but AlterNet says he spent at least ten minutes discussing the pool’s troubled renovation and did not mention the midterms during the first 20 minutes. The outlet also reports that viewers described him as exhausted after a month of campaign travel.

Garrison suggested the behavior could indicate disrupted wakefulness and broader decline, possibly accelerated by a stroke. Those are his interpretations of public footage, not a reported medical diagnosis. The article supplies no examination, medical records, or confirmation that Trump suffered a stroke—or even definitive proof that he was asleep.

Power does not require alertness

The institutional fact is more consequential than the body-language speculation: the person delivering this disjointed address was the president. Trump held executive authority; Burgum served in his administration; the event’s staging placed presidential power behind every wandering minute.

If a president cannot deliver a coherent closing argument without becoming consumed by a renovation project, that is politically relevant. But the relevance comes from the authority attached to the speaker, not from the spectacle of drooping eyelids. A visibly tired private citizen controls little. A president controls an administration whether or not a public appearance inspires confidence.

Diagnosis by video is not accountability

AlterNet’s headline framing promises an “exposure.” The reporting establishes something narrower: one psychologist watched footage and offered an interpretation. Garrison may have relevant expertise, but the article does not establish that he examined Trump or had access to clinical evidence.

That distinction matters because “he appeared to drift off” is an observation; claims about impaired neurological pathways, severe decline, or a possible stroke are medical inferences. Packaging inference as revelation gives sensational certainty to evidence that remains ambiguous.

The strongest criticism requires no remote diagnosis. Trump gave an address meant to close a midterm campaign and, according to AlterNet, failed to mention the election for 20 minutes. That is documented political conduct. Speculating about his nervous system can distract from what he chose—or failed—to communicate while exercising presidential power.

The spectacle displaces the decision-makers

The article turns Trump’s apparent fatigue into the central scandal, leaving the surrounding power structure largely untouched. Someone scheduled the event. Officials stood beside him. Political staff presented the appearance as a closing message. Burgum continued speaking while the president reportedly drifted in and out of attention.

Those actors had agency even if Trump was exhausted or impaired. Yet the coverage treats them as scenery. Institutions often protect themselves this way: attention settles on one leader’s physical condition while the aides and officials who normalize, stage, and sustain the performance escape scrutiny.

A presidency reduced to symptom watching

The fixation on whether Trump was technically asleep offers audiences a simple mystery with an irresistible clip. It is also a political dead end. If he was asleep, the episode raises questions the article does not answer about his capacity and the judgment of those presenting him. If he was merely exhausted, the speech was still unfocused and poorly aligned with its stated purpose.

This is the larger pattern: personality-driven coverage converts failures of governing institutions into medical theater. The president becomes a collection of symptoms; his administration becomes background furniture; responsibility dissolves into frame-by-frame conjecture. The sharper indictment is not that one psychologist saw possible decline. It is that presidential authority remained intact while everyone around it carried on as though coherence were optional.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Your car is being tracked 24/7 — and not for the reasons you think
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that automatic license plate readers are not merely traffic or crime-fighting tools: they feed searchable networks that can reveal where vehicles have traveled. The article does not establish that every car is continuously tracked “24/7,” but it describes systems capable of recording and sharing location data at enormous scale, sometimes beyond the awareness of the municipalities that installed them. In the reporting period, voters in Wellfleet, Massachusetts, unan
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that automatic license plate readers are not merely traffic or crime-fighting tools: they feed searchable networks that can reveal where vehicles have traveled. The article does not establish that every car is continuously tracked “24/7,” but it describes systems capable of recording and sharing location data at enormous scale, sometimes beyond the awareness of the municipalities that installed them.

In the reporting period, voters in Wellfleet, Massachusetts, unanimously banned the technology, and the Selectboard enacted the policy as local law, also prohibiting tracking of boats in town waters. Local police joined activists in concluding that the readers were unnecessary for the town. Similar resistance was reported in Minneapolis, San Diego, and 14 Texas jurisdictions amid concern that federal immigration authorities had obtained plate data while pursuing the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

Flock Safety said cities control data-sharing permissions, its federal pilot program had ended, and ICE could not directly access its databases. But AlterNet cites reporting that federal agencies conducted tens of thousands of lookups or obtained information through other agencies, sometimes without local departments being actively notified about particular searches. The article says the constitutional limits remain unsettled and notes that separate bills backed by Democratic-aligned and Republican lawmakers sought to restrict the systems through federal funding penalties.

The power sits in the network

A camera bolted beside a road is not the central political fact. The database behind it is.

Municipal officials may purchase readers for stolen-car investigations or traffic enforcement, but vendors such as Flock, Axon, and Motorola operate networks that can make local observations available far beyond the locality that collected them. That architecture shifts practical control from the residents being watched—and potentially from their elected officials—to corporations and agencies equipped to search across jurisdictions.

The decisive power is therefore distributed but identifiable. Vendors build and administer the infrastructure. Local governments authorize its installation and set sharing rules. Police departments generate and query records. Federal agencies possess the reach and institutional leverage to seek access. Drivers supply only the data; they make no meaningful choice about its collection.

Consent at the bottom, access at the top

The article’s most important claim is not that officials secretly installed every camera. It is that many local officials reportedly approved systems without understanding the reach of the resulting network.

That is not informed public consent. It is procurement politics: sell a narrow function to a town, then connect the resulting data to a much broader surveillance apparatus. Flock’s position that municipalities control sharing does not resolve reports that federal authorities obtained information without local police being kept apprised of specific searches. A permission screen is a weak safeguard when access can travel through other departments, federal logs, or legal demands whose limits the article says remain unclear.

Wellfleet’s ban shows where agency still exists. The town meeting acted, the Selectboard converted that decision into law, and local police supported the restriction. Institutional helplessness was not the obstacle. Other governments made different choices—or failed to examine what they had purchased.

Public safety is the sales pitch

License plate readers can serve legitimate, concrete purposes. AlterNet notes that one helped locate the suspect in the Brown University shooting far from Providence, and that New York uses plate-reading infrastructure to administer congestion pricing. Those examples establish utility, not a blank check.

The misdirection begins when a successful search in one case is treated as justification for retaining everybody’s movements in a network available for other purposes. The relevant question is not whether a database can help solve a serious crime. Almost any sufficiently intrusive database can. The question is who may search it, under what legal standard, for how long, with whose knowledge, and with what remedy when the system is abused.

“Public safety” collapses those questions into a slogan. It asks residents to judge the most sympathetic use while officials and vendors preserve the capacity for far broader ones.

Surveillance follows political priorities

The reported backlash intensified because immigration enforcement exposed how quickly infrastructure bought for one rationale can serve another. Border and immigration authorities hold federal enforcement power; migrants and people traveling through camera networks do not. Blaming individuals for being “found” by neutral technology would invert responsibility. Governments installed the systems, companies networked the records, and agencies sought the data.

AlterNet also cites reports involving reproductive-health travel and warrantless stalking. Those accounts are not proof that every reader is used that way. They demonstrate the predictable danger of a system designed to reconstruct movement: its uses will follow the priorities—and abuses—of whoever gains access.

The article’s headline overstates its own evidence by implying universal, uninterrupted tracking and by teasing a single hidden reason. The reporting supports a more precise and more consequential conclusion: plate readers create persistent records that can be searched for purposes substantially broader than the local justification offered when the cameras were approved.

The systemic error

This is the familiar conversion of administrative convenience into political power. A town buys a tool. A vendor builds a network. Agencies discover that the network can answer questions residents never authorized them to ask. Each institution points to another part of the chain, and accountability dissolves while the data remain usable.

The bipartisan congressional proposals described by AlterNet differ in sponsorship and scope, but both recognize the same structural problem: local surveillance systems become national systems when databases cross jurisdictional lines. Without firm limits, the actor with the broadest mandate and greatest coercive power gains the advantage.

Wellfleet interrupted that process at its point of entry. Its decision matters not because one small town can dismantle a national surveillance market, but because it rejected the fiction that expansive monitoring is merely a technical upgrade. The cameras record plates. The system records power—and power rarely confines itself to the purpose printed on the purchase order.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: A surreal reality is forcing MAGA Americans to rethink everything
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet argues that voters heading into the November 5, 2026, congressional elections are reacting not merely to higher costs but to the Trump administration’s broader use of federal power. The publication attributes economic pain to tariffs, deportations and war, while describing the administration’s attacks on civil-rights protections, federal institutions and constitutional limits as the election’s central issue. The piece says Hispanic and Black early voting appeared unusually
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet argues that voters heading into the November 5, 2026, congressional elections are reacting not merely to higher costs but to the Trump administration’s broader use of federal power. The publication attributes economic pain to tariffs, deportations and war, while describing the administration’s attacks on civil-rights protections, federal institutions and constitutional limits as the election’s central issue.

The piece says Hispanic and Black early voting appeared unusually strong, though it provides no totals, and interprets that activity as resistance to immigration enforcement and the weakening of voting-rights protections. It also reports concerns about Trump’s public conduct and possible post-election actions, but the article does not establish an election result, a future military escalation or an attempted defiance of the vote.

Power is not a mood

Trump held executive authority. Republicans in Congress held legislative authority and the power to investigate, restrict funding and impose political consequences. The Supreme Court held judicial authority over disputes affecting voting and executive conduct. Voters suffering the consequences did not control any of those institutions.

That distinction matters because “voter anger” is not the cause of this story. It is a response. The relevant decisions were made by officials: the administration imposed tariffs, pursued deportations and exercised military power; congressional Republicans declined to restrain it. AlterNet’s strongest point is that these outcomes should not be flattened into atmospheric dissatisfaction with “the economy.”

The accomplice is Congress

The article places Trump at the center, but its institutional indictment lands most clearly on Republican lawmakers. A president can claim sweeping authority; Congress decides whether to contest that claim, finance it or surrender its own powers.

According to AlterNet, Republicans tolerated the dismantling of agencies, politicization of law enforcement and executive encroachment on spending authority. Some of the publication’s more serious allegations—including self-enrichment, bribery and sham prosecutions—are asserted without enough supporting detail in the supplied text to treat them as established facts. The documented political structure is damning enough: legislators entrusted with checking executive power instead treated restraint as partisan disloyalty.

Economics becomes camouflage

Coverage that reduces the election to prices and broken promises performs a useful misdirection. It presents tariffs, deportations and institutional purges as disconnected policy mistakes rather than exercises of government power with identifiable authors and targets.

Economic framing is attractive because it drains conflict of responsibility. A household budget “feels pressure.” A community “loses confidence.” Costs “rise.” Those formulations conceal the officials who chose the policy and the lawmakers who enabled it. They also push people targeted by state coercion to the margins while centering voters disappointed that coercive politics did not leave their own finances untouched.

AlterNet sometimes overreaches by assigning a single racial motive to a vast electorate. But its underlying criticism holds: political reporting often treats white voters’ material discomfort as the main event and the loss of other citizens’ rights as secondary context.

Diagnosis is not accountability

The article also discusses reporting about Trump’s speech patterns and public behavior, including more digressions and absolutist language. Those observations do not, by themselves, establish dementia. The supplied material offers no medical diagnosis, and using one as settled fact weakens the case.

More importantly, speculation about cognitive decline can become another escape hatch. It converts decisions into symptoms and turns institutional complicity into a story about one man’s condition. Congress did not need a medical assessment to exercise oversight. Courts did not need one to enforce orders. Officials who implemented policy were not powerless spectators to a president’s rhetoric.

The political question is not whether Trump’s conduct can be medically explained. It is why people with constitutional authority continued enabling conduct they could see.

The system rewards surrender

The larger pattern is institutional cowardice packaged as voter analysis. Executive power expands; legislators protect their coalition; courts become election battlegrounds; the press discovers the severity of the situation only when public opinion shifts. Responsibility then migrates downward to “angry voters,” as though citizens created the machinery officials chose to operate.

AlterNet’s argument is most persuasive when it refuses that evasion. The election may impose consequences, but elections do not erase the chain of agency. Trump exercised power. Republican officials enabled him. Major institutions often described the resulting injuries as controversy, confusion or failed policy. That is how deliberate political choices become weather—and how those responsible hope to escape the storm they made.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.
