item.title: Trump’s DOJ crushed in two humiliating court losses before Election Day
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that two federal courts halted the Trump administration’s effort to identify alleged noncitizen voters and pressure election officials handling their ballots. On the Monday before Election Day, the Ninth Circuit vacated a panel ruling that had temporarily freed the Justice Department to threaten local officials with prosecution, restoring U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson’s restraining order while the appeal is reheard en banc. Thompson’s Oct. 30 order barred the
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that two federal courts halted the Trump administration’s effort to identify alleged noncitizen voters and pressure election officials handling their ballots. On the Monday before Election Day, the Ninth Circuit vacated a panel ruling that had temporarily freed the Justice Department to threaten local officials with prosecution, restoring U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson’s restraining order while the appeal is reheard en banc.

Thompson’s Oct. 30 order barred the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security from forcing officials to reject, segregate or set aside ballots solely because a voter might be ineligible. The dispute concerns roughly 20,000 California mail voters whom the Justice Department described as noncitizens; state officials contested both the number and the list’s reliability. The order was set to last through Nov. 16, with another hearing scheduled for Nov. 13.

That same Monday, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan stopped the departments from distributing suspected-noncitizen voter lists to states. She found that plaintiffs were likely to succeed in arguing that the policy exceeded federal authority and violated the Privacy Act. According to her opinion, the lists drew on records covering tens of millions of voters in at least 47 states and included Social Security numbers, birth dates and party affiliations. Plaintiffs alleged that the data produced numerous false positives.

The power came from Washington

The central actors were not confused poll workers or mysterious flaws in “the system.” They were the Justice Department and DHS, wielding federal data, prosecutorial authority and the implied force of criminal investigation immediately before an election.

Bill Essayli, the chief federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, warned that officials knowingly processing a noncitizen’s ballot risked “legal jeopardy.” Whatever the administration’s stated law-enforcement rationale, that warning placed local election workers under federal pressure while the underlying eligibility list remained disputed.

The institutional imbalance is stark. A voter wrongly flagged by a massive database has little practical power to correct the government before a ballot is isolated. A local official threatened with prosecution must weigh lawful ballot counting against personal exposure. The federal government created that pressure; weaker actors were forced to absorb its risks.

Suspicion became the standard

The California order addressed ballots challenged solely because a voter may be ineligible. That distinction is the story’s core. Possible ineligibility is not established ineligibility, and a database match is not an adjudication.

The administration’s approach, as described by AlterNet, joined two mechanisms: distribute lists of purported noncitizens, then bear down on the officials deciding how to treat their ballots. False positives were therefore not a minor technical defect. They were a foreseeable route by which eligible voters could be burdened or excluded at the moment when correction was hardest.

Chutkan’s ruling also exposes the scale of the machinery. Files containing sensitive information on tens of millions of voters across at least 47 states were being used to generate lists for state action. The government’s power rested not merely on what those records proved, but on the authority their official appearance could command.

The framing obscures the stakes

Calling the rulings “humiliating” turns an institutional confrontation into a scorekeeping exercise. The important result was not that the Justice Department suffered an embarrassing day. It was that judges temporarily blocked federal agencies from converting contested data into election instructions and prosecutorial pressure.

The administration portrayed its conduct as law enforcement. The courts did not finally resolve the underlying claims in the proceedings described here: the Ninth Circuit ordered rehearing, Thompson’s restraint was temporary, and Chutkan assessed plaintiffs’ likelihood of success. Precision matters. So does recognizing what had already occurred—the federal government had assembled and sought to circulate the lists while voting was underway.

The weaker framing is a familiar one: contested ballots become the source of disorder, election workers become potential wrongdoers, and the agencies issuing threats disappear behind abstract language about “integrity.” That reverses the chain of responsibility.

A system built to intimidate

This episode reveals how election power can operate before any final legal judgment. Officials with access to national databases can assign suspicion at scale. Prosecutors can make that suspicion personally dangerous for administrators. Even when courts intervene, the government has already forced voters and election workers to navigate uncertainty manufactured from above.

The larger pattern is rule by administrative accusation: label first, distribute the label widely, and make weaker institutions prove why they should not obey it. Judicial restraints can interrupt that process, as they did here. But the systemic failure begins earlier, when unproven government classifications acquire enough coercive force to endanger lawful participation before their accuracy has been established.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Morning Joe wonders if Trump has prediction market bets for GOP losing big
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that MSNBC’s Jonathan Lemire joked that President Donald Trump’s remarks about drainage pipes at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool were so politically damaging that someone should check whether Trump had bet on Democrats through Polymarket. The segment supplied no evidence that Trump or his family placed such a wager; Lemire’s remark was a quip, not an allegation supported by reporting. Joe Scarborough said Republican sources were alarmed by Trump’s closing mess
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that MSNBC’s Jonathan Lemire joked that President Donald Trump’s remarks about drainage pipes at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool were so politically damaging that someone should check whether Trump had bet on Democrats through Polymarket. The segment supplied no evidence that Trump or his family placed such a wager; Lemire’s remark was a quip, not an allegation supported by reporting.

Joe Scarborough said Republican sources were alarmed by Trump’s closing message and broader positions on war, artificial intelligence, tariffs, and healthcare benefits. Former Republican strategist Mark McKinnon argued that the appearance showed nobody in the White House could dissuade Trump from an ineffective message.

The concrete event, then, was not a suspicious bet. It was a president using a prominent Election Day appearance to ramble about infrastructure while Republican observers, as described by the panel, feared major losses.

The joke obscures the power

Trump was not a hapless candidate abandoned by his advisers. He was the president, commanding the country’s largest political stage and exercising dominant influence over the Republican Party. Whatever the electoral effect of his remarks, the institutional power remained his.

The Polymarket joke converts that power into a comic mystery: Could Trump secretly be trying to lose? There is no evidence presented for that theory. More importantly, it distracts from the simpler explanation established by the segment: Trump chose the message, Republican officials lacked the authority or willingness to redirect him, and the party remained bound to his decisions.

Republicans built this dependency

McKinnon’s claim that nobody in the White House could stand up to Trump describes an organizational failure, not an atmospheric condition. Advisers and party officials occupy positions designed to shape decisions, challenge bad strategy, and protect institutional interests. If none could do so, that reflects the structure surrounding Trump: concentrated authority reinforced by people who accepted their own political subordination.

Scarborough’s account of Republicans being “beyond themselves” also grants them too much distance from the outcome. These were not spectators watching an unrelated politician wreck their campaign. They belonged to a party organized around Trump’s leadership. Their alarm came after the dependency was built and when its electoral costs appeared difficult to escape.

Bad strategy is not sabotage

The segment’s most dramatic implication—that Trump’s conduct was so harmful it resembled intentional self-sabotage—was unsupported. A politician can damage his party without secretly betting against it. Personal fixation, poor judgment, indifference to down-ballot candidates, or confidence that loyal audiences will accept any performance can produce the same result.

Calling the behavior inexplicable lets Republican actors avoid a harsher conclusion: they repeatedly enabled a leader whose priorities might not match their own electoral needs. Deliberate sabotage would make them victims. Political submission makes them participants.

The coverage chooses spectacle

AlterNet foregrounds the prediction-market line because it is provocative. But the story’s real political content lies in Scarborough’s report that Republicans believed Trump was hurting them across multiple issues, and in McKinnon’s description of a White House unable to restrain him.

The article also invokes past “suspicious” prediction-market transactions and conspiracy theories about Trump’s family without establishing a connection to this event. That framing adds intrigue while weakening precision. The documented subject is a disastrous closing argument and a powerless—or compliant—Republican apparatus, not insider betting.

A party without corrective machinery

This episode reveals what personalist politics does to a governing party. Policy, campaign strategy, and institutional judgment become subordinate to one leader’s impulses. When the results look ruinous, insiders complain to television hosts, commentators speculate about hidden motives, and responsibility dissolves into astonishment.

The systemic error is not that nobody could understand Trump’s remarks about pipes. It is that a party entrusted its message and fortunes to one man, stripped itself of meaningful internal resistance, and then treated the foreseeable consequences as an unsolved mystery.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Anti-Catholic rhetoric of 1960s is a lot like MAGA hate today: historian
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that historian Barbara A. Perry sees a parallel between the anti-Catholic suspicion John F. Kennedy confronted in 1960 and the anti-Muslim insinuation directed at Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. A Republican operative’s question implied that El-Sayed’s faith made him sympathetic to terrorists and hostile to the United States. El-Sayed answered that he was seeking office as an American who happens to be Muslim, not as a representative of Islam. Pe
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that historian Barbara A. Perry sees a parallel between the anti-Catholic suspicion John F. Kennedy confronted in 1960 and the anti-Muslim insinuation directed at Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. A Republican operative’s question implied that El-Sayed’s faith made him sympathetic to terrorists and hostile to the United States. El-Sayed answered that he was seeking office as an American who happens to be Muslim, not as a representative of Islam.

Perry told AlterNet that Kennedy faced similar claims that a Catholic president would obey the pope rather than the Constitution. She argued that today’s anti-Muslim politics adds an association with terrorism that was absent from most anti-Catholic attacks on Kennedy. At the time of the interview, El-Sayed’s election had not occurred, so the reporting could not establish how much religious prejudice would affect the result.

The interview also connected religious exclusion to government power. Perry argued that the Supreme Court’s conservative majority has moved away from strict church-state separation while Trump and parts of the MAGA movement have promoted a government more explicitly aligned with right-wing Christianity.

The insinuation is the instrument

The operative questioning El-Sayed was not conducting an earnest examination of constitutional loyalty. According to AlterNet’s description, he embedded the accusation inside the question: Muslim identity meant possible allegiance to terrorists and possible hatred of America.

That maneuver makes the target disprove a suspicion created entirely by the accuser. El-Sayed must affirm his constitutional loyalty; the person smearing him is spared any obligation to establish disloyalty. The burden moves from the powerful political movement deploying the stereotype to the minority candidate forced to answer it.

Calling this merely “prejudice” can obscure its political function. The insinuation offers voters a permission structure: they can reject a Muslim candidate while describing their decision as vigilance rather than religious discrimination.

Power belongs to the gatekeepers

El-Sayed has agency over his response, but he did not create the test. Republican operatives and candidates can choose whether to legitimize suspicion of Muslims. Voters decide whether to reward it. Institutions—including parties, courts and government officials—determine whether one religion receives public preference while another is treated as evidence requiring rebuttal.

Perry’s historical comparison is useful precisely because it identifies the asymmetry. Kennedy had to promise that Catholic authorities would not direct his presidency. El-Sayed is being asked to establish that his faith does not compromise his citizenship. Meanwhile, politicians invoking Christianity to shape public institutions are often treated as participants in a normal policy dispute, not as officials whose religious commitments demand a loyalty hearing.

The governing standard is therefore not neutral secularism. It is familiarity backed by power: the dominant faith is presumed compatible with American authority, while the minority faith is made to audition for acceptance.

The Kennedy comparison has limits

AlterNet’s headline compresses a complicated argument into a claim that 1960s anti-Catholic rhetoric resembles “MAGA hate.” The interview supports a narrower conclusion. Both episodes involve imputing foreign religious allegiance to a candidate without evidence. Perry also stressed a major difference: contemporary anti-Muslim rhetoric can exploit the language of terrorism and war.

The article is less disciplined when it treats an eventual El-Sayed defeat as a potential measure of whether Muslims can enter mainstream politics. One election cannot isolate religious bias from party affiliation, policy, campaign quality or other electoral conditions. Perry acknowledged that Michigan cannot simply stand in for the entire United States. The result might supply evidence about a barrier; it could not, by itself, quantify that barrier or prove why voters acted.

Nor does Kennedy’s election show that anti-Catholic power simply vanished. Perry noted later conflicts in which Catholic clergy challenged Catholic politicians over abortion. Barriers can change form while institutions redistribute legitimacy among favored and disfavored believers.

Religious freedom for some

Perry’s account identifies a larger contradiction. Political actors can demand that a Muslim candidate separate personal faith from public authority while supporting greater government accommodation of Christianity. That is not a consistent defense of church-state separation. It is selective suspicion paired with selective privilege.

The Supreme Court holds the strongest institutional power in this part of the story because its rulings set constitutional boundaries for government support of religion. Perry attributes the shift toward accommodation to the Court’s conservative majority, naming Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Samuel Alito, Amy Coney Barrett and Neil Gorsuch among that bloc. Her assessment is an argument about the Court’s direction, not an independently demonstrated finding in the article, but it places responsibility where it belongs: with officials making binding decisions, not only with citizens expressing ugly views.

The political consequence is concrete. When government moves closer to a dominant religious identity, minority candidates do not enter public life on equal terms. They arrive under suspicion, while the majority’s theology is recast as heritage, culture or national identity.

Exclusion keeps changing its target

The durable pattern is not that anti-Muslim politics perfectly repeats anti-Catholic politics. It is that American political movements repeatedly define full citizenship through a religious majority, then force outsiders to prove they are exceptions to the caricature.

Kennedy’s answer was constitutional: public officials owe their authority to voters and their obligations to law, not to clergy. Applied honestly, that principle scrutinizes officials who would use government to privilege Christianity at least as seriously as it scrutinizes a Muslim candidate confronted with an unsupported accusation.

The misdirection begins when coverage centers whether El-Sayed can overcome suspicion rather than who manufactures it, who benefits from it and which institutions reinforce the hierarchy beneath it. The weaker actor is made responsible for surviving the test. The stronger actors retain the power to keep administering it.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Psychotherapist issues chilling warning of 'absolute mess' Trump will create
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that psychotherapist Elliott Connie warned that President Donald Trump would create an “absolute mess” if election losses left him politically cornered. Connie predicted that Trump would reject unfavorable results, pursue lawsuits and recounts, and lash out rather than cooperate with Democrats. These were Connie’s forecasts, not reported events. Connie based that assessment partly on Trump’s election-closing remarks about maintaining the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that psychotherapist Elliott Connie warned that President Donald Trump would create an “absolute mess” if election losses left him politically cornered. Connie predicted that Trump would reject unfavorable results, pursue lawsuits and recounts, and lash out rather than cooperate with Democrats. These were Connie’s forecasts, not reported events.

Connie based that assessment partly on Trump’s election-closing remarks about maintaining the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and possibly attaching his name to it. He said the fixation suggested concern with image and personal recognition rather than public needs.

Connie repeatedly acknowledged that he had not evaluated Trump and could not diagnose him with narcissistic personality disorder. Hillary Clinton separately predicted on The View that Trump would become angry and lash out if congressional power created leverage to hold him accountable. The article supplies no election result or subsequent evidence establishing whether either prediction came true.

The diagnosis is not the evidence

Connie’s caveat matters. Suspecting a disorder is not a clinical diagnosis, and an analysis built around that suspicion cannot convert televised behavior into medical fact. AlterNet foregrounds the psychiatric label anyway, giving a speculative diagnosis more authority than the reporting can support.

The stronger case requires no amateur clinical verdict. Trump’s conduct after the 2020 election—invoked by Connie as the basis for his forecast—is politically relevant because it concerns how a president used his position after losing. The institutional question is not what condition might explain that conduct. It is what Trump did, who enabled him, and whether the safeguards around presidential power held.

Power is the missing subject

Trump holds presidential power. Congress can investigate, legislate, control funding and, under defined constitutional procedures, impose consequences. Courts and election officials can reject unsupported challenges. Party leaders and lawmakers decide whether to reinforce false claims, resist them or remain silent.

Yet the article turns this structure into a personality story. Trump becomes a volatile patient; Clinton and Connie become interpreters of his emotional state; institutions recede into the background. That framing makes public outcomes appear to depend on one man’s temperament when they also depend on officials with concrete authority choosing whether to constrain or assist him.

Prediction replaces accountability

Connie predicted lawsuits, recounts and attempts to invalidate election results. Those are specific possibilities, but AlterNet provides no reported plan, new directive or completed action behind them. The distinction between warning and evidence is essential, especially when the warning concerns future attacks on election outcomes.

Calling the anticipated result an “absolute mess” also obscures agency. A mess sounds accidental. If officials knowingly promote unsupported fraud claims, misuse state power or help overturn lawful results, those are decisions. If courts, legislators or party leaders enable that effort, their participation cannot be reduced to Trump feeling cornered.

The systemic error

The article’s weakest move is to medicalize a political problem. Speculation about narcissism may explain a media persona, but it can also misdirect attention from the people and institutions capable of turning grievance into government action.

The larger pattern is institutional evasion through psychological spectacle. Coverage scrutinizes Trump’s inner life while treating surrounding power brokers as scenery. Democracy is not administered by diagnosis. The consequential facts are who commands public authority, who follows unlawful or unsupported demands, who refuses them, and who pays the price when institutional actors choose loyalty over duty.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump's ultimate get-out-of-jail-free card
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet argues that Donald Trump’s “get-out-of-jail-free card” could be an expanded war with Iran: a crisis severe enough to obstruct a hostile Congress, discourage impeachment, and justify domestic emergency powers. But the article does not establish that Trump has decided to pursue this strategy. Its central claim is a speculative scenario assembled from military planning, political rhetoric, personnel changes, and claims from unnamed sources. The outlet reports that Trump order
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet argues that Donald Trump’s “get-out-of-jail-free card” could be an expanded war with Iran: a crisis severe enough to obstruct a hostile Congress, discourage impeachment, and justify domestic emergency powers. But the article does not establish that Trump has decided to pursue this strategy. Its central claim is a speculative scenario assembled from military planning, political rhetoric, personnel changes, and claims from unnamed sources.

The outlet reports that Trump ordered the Pentagon to develop new strike options against Iran, including possible use of the conventional GBU-43/B bomb, and later said nuclear weapons were unnecessary. It also cites reports of contingency preparations at US bases, the removal of a senior officer involved in war planning, Iranian threats of geographically unrestricted retaliation, and discussions between Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu about another operation. AlterNet presents these developments alongside Trump’s New York felony convictions and Netanyahu’s failure to secure a governing majority as evidence that both leaders could benefit personally from renewed war.

Power, not prophecy

The relevant fact is not that AlterNet has proved a secret plan. It has not. The relevant fact is that presidents command institutions capable of turning political incentives into mass death. Trump can direct military planning and authorize operations; Netanyahu can press for Israeli action against Iran. Iranian leaders control forces capable of retaliation. Civilians possess none of these powers but would absorb the consequences.

That imbalance deserves scrutiny without dressing conjecture as revelation. The reported strike planning is concrete. The claim that its purpose is to prevent Democrats from taking office is an inference. The article repeatedly crosses that boundary, converting alarming circumstances into asserted intent without supplying the evidence needed to close the gap.

The emergency advantage

The political logic described is nevertheless recognizable. War concentrates executive authority, narrows tolerated dissent, and permits leaders to depict oversight as disloyalty. A foreign attack could furnish arguments for troops in American cities, extraordinary election measures, or resistance to impeachment. Those would be choices made by officials, not automatic consequences of national danger.

Trump’s reported warning to House Republicans that losing the midterms could lead to impeachment establishes his concern about congressional power. His New York convictions establish legal exposure beyond federal pardon authority, although the article says sentencing was frozen after his election. Neither fact proves that military planning is designed to preserve his freedom. They do establish an incentive that Congress, the press, and military officials should examine with considerably more rigor than AlterNet provides.

Evidence strained past its limit

The article’s weakest move is to treat nearly every disturbing development as another piece of one coordinated plot. Base-resilience requirements become evidence of a timeline extending beyond the seating of Congress. A general’s disputed removal becomes the clearing of an obstacle because he supposedly possessed “veto power.” Iranian retaliation planning becomes the desired trigger for domestic repression.

Those connections may warrant investigation. They do not warrant certainty. Military contingency planning, infrastructure preparation, and command reshuffling can be ominous without proving a scheme to manufacture an attack on the United States. A serious charge requires documents, attributable testimony, or a demonstrable chain of orders. Accumulating suspicions does not substitute for establishing causation.

The framing also strips agency from institutions that would have to enable such an outcome. The Pentagon is not weather. Congress is not furniture. Courts, state governments, military commanders, and federal officers would each face decisions about unlawful orders, election interference, domestic deployment, and emergency authority. Presenting Trump as an omnipotent conspirator can inadvertently excuse everyone whose cooperation would be required.

The system behind the scenario

The larger danger lies in the lawful machinery available before any imagined conspiracy begins. A president can request catastrophic strike options. Advisers can normalize them as contingency planning. Legislators can surrender scrutiny once troops are committed. Media organizations can repeat claims of necessity while treating the resulting civilian deaths as strategic abstractions.

That system does not need an “apocalyptic” mastermind to produce disaster. It needs concentrated war powers, pliant officials, weak oversight, and a political culture that grants leaders more deference precisely when their incentives demand more suspicion.

AlterNet identifies a legitimate question—whether leaders under personal political pressure might exploit war—but weakens it by presenting inference as near-certainty. The sharper indictment is less cinematic: institutions have made it possible for officials with obvious conflicts of interest to approach decisions of immense consequence while the public is left to reconstruct intent from threats, leaks, firings, and contingency plans. That is not proof of the plot alleged here. It is proof of a power structure built to conceal responsibility until after the damage is done.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Federal judge maps out stunning plan to catch Trump officials mid-lie
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened A federal judge in Oregon urged trial courts to require ICE officers to testify in person when their accounts are disputed, allowing examination and cross-examination rather than relying only on written declarations. AlterNet reports that Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai issued that recommendation Monday after finding that an ICE officer gave false information in official arrest records and then minimized it as an oversight under oath. Kasubhai wrote that ICE personnel conducted warrantle
item.content:encoded:
What happened

A federal judge in Oregon urged trial courts to require ICE officers to testify in person when their accounts are disputed, allowing examination and cross-examination rather than relying only on written declarations. AlterNet reports that Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai issued that recommendation Monday after finding that an ICE officer gave false information in official arrest records and then minimized it as an oversight under oath.

Kasubhai wrote that ICE personnel conducted warrantless arrests without adequately establishing probable cause that people posed an escape risk, violating a preliminary injunction. He said the evidence ranged from typographical errors to fabrication and raised doubts about ICE arrest forms across Oregon, while noting that other courts have identified falsehoods and errors in ICE documentation elsewhere.

The ruling did not unveil a scheme to catch unnamed “Trump officials” in spontaneous lies. It described a conventional accountability mechanism—sworn testimony tested against records—and explained why courts should use it when government declarations cannot be trusted.

Power sits with the arresting agency

ICE agents exercise coercive state power. They can detain people, create the records used to justify those detentions, and supply courts with the government’s account afterward. The people arrested must then challenge a narrative produced by the same institution that seized them.

That imbalance makes false documentation more than an administrative defect. An inaccurate government form can become the foundation for continued detention or the supposed legal justification for an arrest. When officials control both the coercive act and its initial record, scrutiny cannot end with accepting their paperwork.

The misconduct was institutional, not mysterious

Kasubhai found that defendants violated his preliminary injunction. He also found that the one testifying officer falsely recorded facts about an arrest. Those are decisions and actions by government personnel, not confusion generated by an immigration system too complicated for anyone to understand.

The evidence cited does not establish how many other Oregon agents committed similar misconduct. Kasubhai said precisely that there was “no telling” how many did. But uncertainty about the scale does not diminish the proven failure; it explains why untested declarations are inadequate.

The headline oversells the novelty

AlterNet’s framing turns basic judicial fact-finding into a “stunning plan” aimed at Trump officials. That language personalizes and sensationalizes a problem the ruling presents as structural: federal agents made warrantless arrests, produced deficient records, and operated in violation of a court order.

Live testimony is not an ingenious trap. It is ordinary adjudication. Calling it stunning inadvertently reveals how weak accountability has become: requiring armed federal officers to answer questions under oath now looks extraordinary.

The framing also risks shifting attention from the people exercising power to the judge’s method of exposing them. The important event is not that Kasubhai devised a clever way to catch a lie. It is that an ICE officer’s official account failed when tested, and that the agency’s documentation practices were serious enough to cast doubt on a broader body of records.

Paperwork can conceal coercion

Government declarations carry institutional authority even when their factual basis is thin. Courts that treat those documents as presumptively reliable allow executive agencies to convert their own assertions into legal insulation.

Kasubhai’s answer is procedural but consequential: put the responsible officer on the stand, compare the testimony with the documents, and permit cross-examination. That does not guarantee truth. It removes one layer of protection from officials whose written claims might otherwise escape meaningful challenge.

Accountability cannot remain optional

The larger pattern is institutional deference to executive enforcement. Agencies act first, document their justification, and depend on courts and the public lacking the time or machinery to test each account. Weak scrutiny rewards that arrangement whether a false record results from carelessness or fabrication.

Kasubhai’s ruling identifies the necessary allocation of responsibility. The government must substantiate the coercion it exercises; detained people should not bear the impossible burden of disproving official paperwork from outside the room where it was created. When sworn testimony is treated as a remarkable escalation, the systemic error is already visible: state power has been trusted more readily than it has been examined.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: MAGA’s desperate plot to avert disaster dead on arrival in court: law expert
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that the Center for Renewing America proposed blocking certain victorious Democratic candidates from taking their congressional seats by arguing that their politics or religion make them incapable of sincerely supporting the Constitution. The group’s legal fellow, Benjamin Osborne, advanced the proposal after executive director Wade Miller had placed several progressive and Muslim politicians within a supposed “Red-Green Alliance.” Constitutional scholars interview
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Center for Renewing America proposed blocking certain victorious Democratic candidates from taking their congressional seats by arguing that their politics or religion make them incapable of sincerely supporting the Constitution. The group’s legal fellow, Benjamin Osborne, advanced the proposal after executive director Wade Miller had placed several progressive and Muslim politicians within a supposed “Red-Green Alliance.”

Constitutional scholars interviewed by WIRED said the scheme would fail in court. Brown University’s Corey Brettschneider cited the Constitution’s prohibition on religious tests, while NYU law professor Richard Pildes said flatly that it would not happen. The Supreme Court’s 1969 ruling in Powell v. McCormack also established that the House cannot exclude a member-elect who meets the Constitution’s age, citizenship, and residency requirements.

USC political scientist Christian Grose nevertheless warned that Republicans might contest a narrow Democratic Senate victory, potentially dragging litigation into the new Congress. The article does not report that any congressional leader adopted the proposal or that a lawsuit was filed.

The power behind the proposal

This is not merely an eccentric argument posted by an irrelevant crank. The Center for Renewing America was founded by Russell Vought, whom AlterNet identifies as a Project 2025 architect and President Donald Trump’s budget director. That connection does not prove the administration or congressional Republicans endorsed Osborne’s proposal. It does establish that the idea emerged from an organization with access to governing circles.

The decisive institutional power would belong to Republican lawmakers attempting to deny seats, party officials supporting election challenges, and courts asked to stop them. Muslim and progressive candidates are the targets, not the actors controlling the machinery. Any framing that treats this as a dispute between equally empowered ideological camps obscures who could actually convert rhetoric into exclusion.

Bigotry dressed as constitutional fidelity

The proposal’s logic is straightforwardly discriminatory: label political opponents “neo-Marxist,” combine that label with an attack on “anti-Western Muslims,” and then declare the targets constitutionally untrustworthy. AlterNet notes that some of the people named are democratic socialists but none identifies as Marxist. The category is therefore not a careful description. It is a polemical container built to make disfavored citizens appear presumptively disloyal.

Applied to Muslims, the maneuver collides directly with the Constitution’s ban on religious tests for office. The Constitution is being invoked as the instrument for doing what it expressly forbids. That is not legal confusion. It is an exclusionary political demand wearing borrowed constitutional language.

Losing the case can still serve the campaign

Calling the plan “dead on arrival” answers the narrow legal question while understating the political function. Brettschneider suggested the group may be testing whether the argument will “stick” and said unsuccessful actions can still intimidate opponents. Grose identified a concrete vulnerability: a close Senate result could invite a contest that outlasts the election and disrupts the opening of Congress.

A meritless theory can therefore produce consequences before a final judgment arrives. It can delay recognition of electoral outcomes, force winners to spend time and money defending their seats, and teach supporters to regard lawful victories by ideological or religious opponents as inherently illegitimate. Courts may reject the claim without undoing every institutional and political cost created by advancing it.

The real target is electoral legitimacy

The deeper pattern is the conversion of defeat into alleged disqualification. Under this logic, voters may choose the “wrong” representative, but a better-positioned faction reserves the power to declare that choice constitutionally invalid. Elections remain acceptable only when they produce approved winners.

The reporting does not establish that this proposal became Republican policy or an operative legal challenge. It does show a well-connected right-wing organization circulating a rationale for excluding elected opponents, with Muslims singled out through an argument the Constitution specifically bars. The systemic danger lies in that rehearsal: manufacture an enemy category, redefine political difference as disloyalty, and use institutional delay as a substitute for winning consent.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Shocking new report reveals half of the military wants to quit over Trump
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that a Common Defense poll found 53 percent of surveyed active-duty service members said increasing politicization made them want to leave military service sooner. Separately, 45 percent said Trump administration policy changes and uncertainty had them considering departure. That supports concern about retention, but not the headline’s simplified claim that half the entire military wants to quit specifically “over Trump.” The poll also found 67 percent of responden
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that a Common Defense poll found 53 percent of surveyed active-duty service members said increasing politicization made them want to leave military service sooner. Separately, 45 percent said Trump administration policy changes and uncertainty had them considering departure. That supports concern about retention, but not the headline’s simplified claim that half the entire military wants to quit specifically “over Trump.”

The poll also found 67 percent of respondents believed decisions affecting service members were being made for political gain rather than mission readiness. About half of veterans and active-duty respondents disapproved of President Donald Trump as commander-in-chief, while 47 percent approved; Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth received similarly divided ratings.

AlterNet connects that dissatisfaction to Hegseth’s leadership, depleted munitions, conflict with Iran, and the removal or sidelining of more than 80 generals and admirals. It highlights the dismissal of Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, which The New York Times reported angered current and retired senior Army officers. The supplied reporting does not include the poll’s sample size, field dates, sampling method, or margin of error.

The headline outruns the evidence

“Half the military wants to quit over Trump” compresses two different findings into a cleaner and more explosive claim. Fifty-three percent reportedly linked an accelerated departure to politicization; 45 percent reportedly cited Trump-era policy changes and uncertainty. “Want to separate sooner” also does not necessarily mean an immediate plan to resign.

Those distinctions do not erase the warning. They define it accurately. If the poll is representative, a large share of active-duty personnel sees political interference as damaging enough to affect career decisions. But AlterNet withholds the methodological information readers would need to judge that premise. A readiness argument built on polling should disclose whose responses are being generalized to the force.

Power sits at the top

Service members do not appoint the defense secretary, remove senior commanders, or decide whether personnel policy will serve operational needs or culture-war politics. Trump holds commander-in-chief authority. Hegseth exercises civilian control over the Defense Department. Their decisions—not the discontent those decisions produce—are the relevant exercise of institutional power.

The reported removal or sidelining of more than 80 generals and admirals is therefore not atmospheric “uncertainty.” It is an identifiable leadership practice. The Times reportedly said most were given no reason. That does not establish that every dismissal was improper, but it does reveal a system in which senior expertise can be discarded without a publicly stated operational rationale.

Dissatisfaction is not the cause

Political coverage often treats collapsing morale as though it were an unfortunate force of nature. Troops become unhappy. Officers lose confidence. Readiness somehow deteriorates. That grammar launders agency.

The poll respondents instead identified decisions made for political gain as the problem. Common Defense executive director Jose Vasquez called the result a readiness crisis, but he is an advocate interpreting his organization’s survey, not a neutral auditor establishing military capacity. AlterNet should preserve that distinction while still following the chain of responsibility: civilian leaders set policy, commanders administer it, and service members absorb the consequences.

Culture war has material costs

Hegseth’s reported emphasis on culture-war issues matters because political spectacle competes with the military’s actual functions. Leadership churn can disrupt planning, weaken institutional memory, and signal that political compatibility carries more weight than accumulated expertise. Those are foreseeable risks even when the motives behind individual dismissals remain unproven.

AlterNet also invokes depleted munitions and failures connected to the war with Iran, but supplies too little specific evidence here to measure those claims. The stronger argument does not require embellishment: when personnel say politicization is influencing whether they remain in uniform, political management has already become a readiness issue.

The systemic error

The deeper pattern is the conversion of public institutions into instruments of personal and ideological control, followed by surprise when those institutions lose experienced people and operational capacity. Authority stays concentrated at the top; blame drifts downward toward supposedly disaffected workers, resistant professionals, or an institution portrayed as mysteriously dysfunctional.

The poll cannot, on the information supplied, prove that half the armed forces will leave. It does show reported distrust on a scale that civilian leadership cannot plausibly dismiss as a communications problem. When leaders privilege political gain over institutional competence, the resulting damage is not confusion. It is the predictable bill for how they chose to govern.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump rants about disproven pool vandals before crowd of dozens
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used his final address before Election Day to reopen the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and again blame vandals for damage that the government’s own investigation reportedly attributed to contractor errors. Speaking on the Monday before the election to a small gathering of National Park Service staff, White House officials, and journalists, Trump also floated renaming the pool after himself, then said he was kidding and asked that the
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used his final address before Election Day to reopen the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and again blame vandals for damage that the government’s own investigation reportedly attributed to contractor errors. Speaking on the Monday before the election to a small gathering of National Park Service staff, White House officials, and journalists, Trump also floated renaming the pool after himself, then said he was kidding and asked that the remark not be reported.

According to AlterNet, the no-bid contractor acknowledged that its mistakes caused the new liner to peel and tear. Federal prosecutors nevertheless charged former Olympian David Hearn, but U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro dropped the case after the government’s evidence contradicted its accusation. A judge then dismissed the case with prejudice, preventing prosecutors from reviving it.

Trump continued claiming that people had slashed the liner with knives, criticized Pirro for “folding,” and repeatedly credited his administration with fixing the pool. AlterNet says his remarks concentrated on the pool, crime in Washington, and other projects despite polling indicating that voters believed he was focused on the wrong priorities.

Power made the accusation dangerous

Trump was not merely a spectator repeating a rumor. He controlled the executive branch whose Justice Department prosecuted Hearn, and Pirro—described by AlterNet as his longtime ally—led the office that brought the charge. The institutional imbalance could hardly be clearer: the president had a national platform and federal law enforcement; the accused individual had to survive a case built by the state.

The dismissal with prejudice matters because it shows that an ordinary retreat by prosecutors was not enough. According to the reporting, the judge acted to prevent the administration from trying again. That is a stark institutional response to the possibility that prosecutorial power could outlive the evidence supporting its use.

The failure belonged to the administration

The decisive act was the administration’s choice to convert a contractor failure into a criminal accusation. AlterNet reports that the contractor—whose owner was a Republican donor and a neighbor of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort—admitted its own errors damaged the liner. The article does not establish that the contract was corrupt, but it does establish a politically relevant sequence: a favored, no-bid arrangement failed, and blame was directed at an alleged vandal instead.

That shift protected the administration’s preferred story. A botched renovation raises questions about procurement, competence, and accountability. A vandalism narrative replaces those questions with a simpler spectacle: dangerous outsiders attacked a presidential achievement. The weaker actor becomes the problem while the officials who selected the contractor retain control of the explanation.

Disproven claims became political theater

Trump’s continued insistence was not confusion created by ambiguous evidence. As AlterNet presents it, prosecutors abandoned the case because their own investigation contradicted the charge, and the contractor acknowledged responsibility for the physical failure. Trump then attacked Pirro for dropping the prosecution and repeated the vandalism claim anyway.

His reference to a Fox News segment illustrates how the narrative sustained itself. Government officials supplied an accusation; friendly media amplified it; the resulting coverage was then invoked as validation. That loop does not make the underlying claim stronger. It allows political authority and media repetition to impersonate evidence after the legal case has collapsed.

The crowd was not the consequence

AlterNet emphasizes Trump’s low energy and the gathering’s small size. Those details describe a weak campaign tableau, but they are not the central political fact. Crowd size is fleeting. The use of federal prosecution to advance a false account of an administrative failure carries consequences for the person charged and for every official deciding whether evidence or presidential anger should govern their conduct.

The article’s ridicule risks shrinking an abuse of power into a story about a rambling performance. Trump’s vanity and fixation are relevant, especially when he jokes about attaching his name to a national landmark. But the sharper story is that presidential self-glorification was backed by institutions capable of investigating, charging, and repeatedly pursuing a designated culprit.

The systemic error

This episode shows how authoritarian scapegoating can begin with something as petty as a torn pool liner. A government failure is recast as sabotage. A politically useful suspect is charged. Contrary evidence becomes disloyalty. A collapsed prosecution is treated not as correction, but as weakness by the prosecutor.

The system’s partial safeguards worked here: the charges were dropped, and a judge barred their resurrection. But the president retained the platform to repeat the allegation without presenting new evidence. That is the larger pattern: institutional power manufactures a grievance, weaker actors bear the legal risk, allied media circulate the claim, and accountability is diverted from the officials who made the consequential decisions.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Republican analyst calls it: Trump has 'doomed' the GOP
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that conservative Washington Post columnist Henry Olsen blamed President Donald Trump’s weak approval for what he predicted would be a devastating Republican midterm defeat. Writing on the Monday before Election Day, Olsen forecast that Democrats would win both chambers of Congress, while Republicans would also lose governorships and state legislative chambers. These were predictions, not reported election results. Olsen projected a 9.25-point Democratic advantage
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that conservative Washington Post columnist Henry Olsen blamed President Donald Trump’s weak approval for what he predicted would be a devastating Republican midterm defeat. Writing on the Monday before Election Day, Olsen forecast that Democrats would win both chambers of Congress, while Republicans would also lose governorships and state legislative chambers. These were predictions, not reported election results.

Olsen projected a 9.25-point Democratic advantage in the national House vote, a 20-seat Democratic gain to 235 seats, and a Democratic Senate takeover. His model began with Trump’s reported 38.8 percent approval rating and historical comparisons between presidential approval and midterm voting. He allowed that late Democratic scandals could affect races but argued that many opinions—and votes—were already fixed.

AlterNet’s headline turns Olsen’s grim forecast into a definitive verdict that Trump has “doomed” the GOP. Olsen’s actual position was narrower: he expected a terrible election, but explicitly said the Trump era might survive and the party could recover, as it did after 1976 and 2008.

Power belongs to the party in office

Republicans are not spectators trapped aboard Trump’s sinking ship. They are the governing party Olsen describes as facing punishment for “the course of Trump’s presidency.” Trump holds presidential power; Republican legislators, candidates, and party officials chose whether to support, excuse, or resist his administration.

That distinction matters. A president can dominate a party, but domination still depends on institutional cooperation. If Republicans lose power, the consequence belongs not only to Trump’s unpopularity but also to the officials who tied their offices to him and helped sustain his political direction.

A forecast is not a result

The article presents a detailed model, but its framing repeatedly slides toward certainty. Approval ratings and historical voting patterns can support a forecast; they cannot convert votes that have not been counted into an accomplished Democratic majority.

Olsen acknowledged a range of possible outcomes and described his numbers as projections. AlterNet sharpened that conditional analysis into “doom.” That makes the story more dramatic while making it less precise. The established fact is Trump’s reported 38.8 percent approval in Olsen’s cited measure. The House margin, seat count, Senate takeover, and down-ballot losses remained predictions at the time described.

Blame is narrowed too neatly

Calling Trump the sole author of Republican collapse risks laundering the agency of the rest of the party. Republican officeholders benefit when Trump mobilizes voters, advances their policies, and attacks their opponents. Declaring themselves his helpless casualties only when the bargain becomes electorally expensive is evasion.

The stronger interpretation is collective responsibility with unequal power. Trump is the party’s president and central political force. Republican officials are the enablers who made his dominance operational. Voters may punish the brand from the top down, but the conduct being judged was maintained across institutions.

The party is not the casualty

Olsen’s imagery casts Republican candidates as troops headed toward destruction. But losing an election is not annihilation; it is removal from public power. The concrete stakes are control of Congress, state governments, and the authority those offices exercise over millions of people.

This is where horse-race coverage misdirects attention. It encourages readers to experience an election through the anguish of incumbents and strategists rather than through the consequences of their governance. The relevant question is not how horrific defeat feels to Republicans. It is why the public, according to Olsen’s analysis, had become so dissatisfied with the presidency their party upheld.

Electoral punishment is not structural change

Olsen’s own historical comparison undercuts the deathbed language. Republicans recovered after Watergate-era defeat and after the Iraq War and economic collapse, then pushed American politics further in their direction. A bad election can cost a party offices without dismantling the institutions, donor networks, media systems, or incentives that produced its conduct.

That is the systemic lesson: parties routinely personalize collective failure so they can survive it. Trump becomes the entire explanation, other Republican actors become collateral damage, and defeat becomes a temporary navigation problem. Accountability begins by rejecting that fiction. Political power was exercised through a party, not by one man acting alone.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Even conservatives are bashing 'out of touch' Trump’s bizarre closing speech
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used his final public address before the 2026 midterm voting began not to make a sustained case about the election, but to defend the renovation of the Reflecting Pool near the Lincoln Memorial. According to journalists monitoring the Washington event, he spent at least the first 20 minutes discussing the pool, including its pipes, paint and algae, while repeating claims that its problems resulted from vandalism—claims AlterNet describes
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used his final public address before the 2026 midterm voting began not to make a sustained case about the election, but to defend the renovation of the Reflecting Pool near the Lincoln Memorial. According to journalists monitoring the Washington event, he spent at least the first 20 minutes discussing the pool, including its pipes, paint and algae, while repeating claims that its problems resulted from vandalism—claims AlterNet describes as debunked.

The speech drew ridicule from Democratic figures, journalists and anti-Trump conservatives including Bill Kristol and Tom Nichols. Their shared criticism was that Trump appeared consumed by a vanity project and personal grievances while his party faced a difficult election. AlterNet also reports that some observers disputed Trump’s attempt to minimize the algae problem, noting that algae naturally recedes after summer.

The article cites a digitally altered image circulated by House Majority PAC showing a pollster’s prediction that Democrats had a 92 percent chance of winning the House. That forecast was not an election result, and the reporting supplied here does not establish what ultimately happened at the polls.

The power was at the microphone

Trump was not an irrelevant eccentric wandering into a national monument with unsolicited maintenance opinions. He was the president, addressing voters on behalf of a party whose candidates depended on his political operation. He held the institutional power to set executive priorities, command public attention and shape the Republican campaign’s closing message.

That distinction matters because “out of touch” can sound like a diagnosis of accidental disconnection. The reported conduct was more concrete: the president chose to devote scarce political time to defending a renovation associated with his administration and rebutting criticism of it. Whatever his private motive, the public decision centered his grievance rather than the material concerns AlterNet says were driving voters.

Mockery is not accountability

The jokes were easy because the spectacle was absurd. Algae, pipes and paint are rich material when a president is supposed to be explaining why voters should preserve his party’s power.

But a parade of sarcastic posts can shrink a political failure into a content failure. The problem was not merely that Trump delivered a bad “closing argument.” It was that presidential authority had become a stage for personal vindication. Treating that chiefly as bizarre campaign theater lets the institution disappear behind the performance.

The anti-Trump conservatives quoted by AlterNet recognized the tactical disaster. Their criticism, however, remained largely electoral: his party might lose because he could not stay on message. That is not the same as confronting why a governing party permitted its closing appeal to revolve around one man’s resentments.

The party enabled the grievance machine

The reporting does not identify who planned the venue, approved the material or tried to redirect the speech, so it cannot support claims about any particular aide’s role. What it does show is that Trump delivered this address as the Republican Party’s dominant national figure after campaigning across heavily Republican states.

That makes Republican candidates and officials more than innocent bystanders to an embarrassing monologue. They had organized their electoral project around a leader whose personal fixations routinely consumed the political agenda. Their immediate lack of control was the foreseeable cost of their longer submission.

Anonymous Republicans reportedly were expected to dislike the message. Anonymity is part of the structure here: powerful party actors preserve access by withholding public criticism, then complain privately when the leader they enabled becomes an electoral liability.

The article’s own misdirection

AlterNet’s framing is strongest when it identifies the mismatch between voter concerns and Trump’s fixation. It is weaker when it relies on online mockery to carry the case. “Even conservatives” objecting is not the decisive evidence. Conservative disapproval does not make a presidential failure more real, and tactical embarrassment is not a substitute for examining power.

The crowd size and the strangeness of the subject may signal political weakness, but they should not obscure institutional strength. Trump still possessed the presidency and the platform that came with it. Weaker actors—voters worried about the economy, candidates tethered to his movement and the public subjected to the administration’s priorities—would bear consequences that the pundits making algae jokes would not.

A system built around one man

The larger pattern is personalization of state and party power. A public landmark becomes an extension of the president’s image; criticism of its renovation becomes a grievance requiring presidential rebuttal; an election becomes another occasion to defend the leader’s judgment.

That system does not fail only when the leader loses focus. The fixation is the governing logic: institutions, campaigns and public attention are reorganized around protecting one person from embarrassment. The algae was trivial. The concentration of power that made it a presidential closing argument was not.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump showing unusual new signs of exhaustion: White House veteran
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that White House correspondent Paula Reid saw an unusual decline in President Donald Trump’s stamina immediately before the midterm elections. On a Monday MS NOW broadcast, Reid cited his complaints about fatigue, travel, and his voice, along with his reduced rally schedule. Reid argued that exhaustion likely helped explain Trump’s decision to deliver his closing message at Washington’s Lincoln Memorial rather than campaign in contested states. She called the locat
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that White House correspondent Paula Reid saw an unusual decline in President Donald Trump’s stamina immediately before the midterm elections. On a Monday MS NOW broadcast, Reid cited his complaints about fatigue, travel, and his voice, along with his reduced rally schedule.

Reid argued that exhaustion likely helped explain Trump’s decision to deliver his closing message at Washington’s Lincoln Memorial rather than campaign in contested states. She called the location a political “safe space,” noting that Trump discussed the Reflecting Pool’s renovation and grass while congressional control—and the prospect of oversight involving his administration, allies, and family—hung in the balance.

The report offers Reid’s interpretation, not medical evidence or an account from White House decision-makers. It does not establish why the venue was selected. It establishes that an experienced correspondent observed a change and regarded the campaign choice as conspicuously weak.

Power does not disappear with stamina

Trump held the presidency. According to Reid, he had governed with little congressional restraint. That institutional fact matters more than whether he looked energetic on television.

Exhaustion may explain diminished campaigning, but it does not transfer responsibility. The president still controlled the executive branch, and his party still depended on him to defend its congressional position. Choosing symbolic comfort over electoral work was consequential precisely because the person making—or accepting—that choice possessed enormous power.

The refuge of spectacle

Reid’s “safe space” description identifies a familiar political maneuver: retreat from an uncontrollable contest into a setting built for managed imagery. Elections, oversight, and vulnerable races cannot be landscaped into submission. A renovation can.

That does not prove the venue was chosen to avoid political danger. But the contrast reported by AlterNet is stark. With Texas and Michigan presented as consequential terrain, Trump focused attention on the Reflecting Pool and the condition of its grass. The presidency became a backdrop for a builder persona while the actual political stakes remained elsewhere.

Fatigue is not the central failure

The article’s exhaustion frame risks turning a strategic failure into a story about personal stamina. Being tired is not an abuse of power. Using the final campaign window poorly while allies face electoral danger is a decision with political consequences.

The sharper question is not whether Trump had enough energy. It is why a governing coalition organized so much of its identity and electoral machinery around one man’s appetite for performance. When that appetite weakened, the party apparently had no equivalent source of momentum. Personal rule produces institutional fragility by design.

The grass is the misdirection

Peter Alexander reportedly noted that the Reflecting Pool renovation had become associated with waste and incompetence. Even so, the discussion remained fixed on venue selection, optics, and Trump’s mood.

That framing can obscure the underlying power struggle: congressional control would determine whether an administration Reid described as largely unchecked faced meaningful scrutiny. Grass was trivial; oversight was not. Treating the episode primarily as an eccentric campaign choice risks repeating the same displacement the event itself embodied—substituting scenery and temperament for accountability.

A system built around one performer

This story reveals the weakness of politics organized around personal dominance. A party that benefits from a president’s rallies also inherits his fatigue, preferences, evasions, and fixation on familiar symbols.

The systemic error is larger than one depleted performance. Institutions surrendered political agency to a single figure, then encountered the predictable consequence: when he withdrew toward spectacle, the coalition followed, and questions of governing power were left standing behind him, out of frame.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump in ‘fragile’ state as GOP leaks reveal his rallies bombed
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Salon writer Amanda Marcotte described Donald Trump as being in a “real fragile state, narcissism-wise” after he attacked a reporter who asked about canceled campaign rallies and his health. Trump called the reporter “disgusting,” insisted he felt “perfect,” and later restored the rallies. The report says Republican candidates in several states privately wanted Trump to stay away because they believed his policies, approval ratings, and appearances were hurtin
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Salon writer Amanda Marcotte described Donald Trump as being in a “real fragile state, narcissism-wise” after he attacked a reporter who asked about canceled campaign rallies and his health. Trump called the reporter “disgusting,” insisted he felt “perfect,” and later restored the rallies.

The report says Republican candidates in several states privately wanted Trump to stay away because they believed his policies, approval ratings, and appearances were hurting them with swing voters. Marcotte cited smaller crowds and polling declines around some candidates, while Politico reported that Republican lawmakers were questioning Trump’s ability to dictate electoral outcomes. The article does not establish the midterm results; it says Senate contests remained uncertain and Republicans expected Trump to blame others if they lost.

The power behind the panic

Trump held the institutional power described here. He controlled the White House, commanded the party’s attention, and could impose himself on campaigns whose candidates apparently believed his presence was politically damaging. Those candidates had agency: they could reject an appearance or publicly challenge him. According to the reporting, they declined to do so.

That distinction matters. This was not merely a domineering leader surrounded by helpless subordinates. It was a party structure in which elected Republicans calculated that humiliation and electoral damage were safer than resistance. Trump reportedly mocked Ken Paxton’s appearance and ridiculed Jon Husted while they stood beside him and smiled. Their submission was political behavior, not weather.

Cowardice disguised as leakage

The leaks described by AlterNet are not evidence that Republicans had reclaimed control of their party. They are evidence that some wanted distance from Trump without accepting the cost of creating it.

Anonymous complaints let lawmakers advertise private misgivings while preserving public obedience. If Trump’s rallies were damaging candidates, the consequential decision was not his insistence on appearing. It was their willingness to host him anyway. The weaker actors in this story were not Republican officeholders with platforms, donors, and votes. They were the voters being subjected to a party that concealed its own assessment of its leader until electoral consequences appeared imminent.

The psychology is not the mechanism

The article leans heavily on Marcotte’s psychological interpretation of Trump’s reaction. His outburst may support her view that he cannot tolerate suggestions of weakness, but a remote diagnosis is less politically useful than the conduct in plain sight.

Trump answered a legitimate question with a personal attack. Advisers reportedly limited his exposure to unwelcome information. Republican candidates feared his intervention yet accommodated it. Those are observable choices and institutional failures. Focusing too narrowly on whether Trump felt psychologically “fragile” risks turning a system of incentives and capitulation into a personality drama.

Accountability, preassigned elsewhere

Republicans quoted by Politico expected Trump to reject responsibility for losses, and Marcotte said his speeches and social-media posts were already identifying alternative culprits, including Fox News. That is not confusion about causation. It is advance construction of an alibi, according to the reporting.

But the party’s lawmakers were preparing alibis of their own. By leaking that Trump had become a liability, they positioned themselves to blame him after an adverse result without explaining why they continued enabling him before it. Trump’s reflexive scapegoating and their anonymous self-exoneration serve the same purpose: preserving power by assigning consequences elsewhere.

A party built to evade consequences

The larger pattern is institutional cowardice dressed up as strategic concern. Republican officials reportedly recognized a political liability, possessed the authority to resist it, and chose accommodation while privately complaining to journalists.

A leader insulated from bad news is dangerous to competent government, but the insulation does not build itself. Aides supply flattery. Candidates accept public degradation. Lawmakers whisper what they refuse to say under their own names. The systemic error is not that one politician cannot bear bad news. It is that an entire governing party can recognize reality, suppress its response, and then compete to escape responsibility for the result.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump hit by last-minute 'brutal' humiliation before Election Day
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that the “humiliation” was a set of New York Times/Siena College polls showing Democratic Senate candidates ahead in seven battleground states on the Monday before Election Day. The label came from the Daily Beast’s description of the results as a “brutal outlook” for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. The reported leads ranged from two points in Alaska to eleven in Michigan. Across the seven states, 38 percent of likely voters approved of Trump’s pre
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the “humiliation” was a set of New York Times/Siena College polls showing Democratic Senate candidates ahead in seven battleground states on the Monday before Election Day. The label came from the Daily Beast’s description of the results as a “brutal outlook” for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

The reported leads ranged from two points in Alaska to eleven in Michigan. Across the seven states, 38 percent of likely voters approved of Trump’s presidential performance, while respondents favored Democrats on living costs, foreign wars, and the interests of ordinary people. These were polling results, not election results; the article supplies neither methodology nor evidence that Trump alone caused every Republican deficit.

Power was on the ballot

The institutional prize was control of the Senate and, with it, the capacity to constrain or reinforce Trump during the final two years of his presidency. Voters had agency, but candidates, party organizations, donors, and the president possessed the machinery: money, endorsements, rallies, and national messaging.

Trump exercised that power conspicuously. AlterNet says he campaigned for Ken Paxton in Texas, appeared for Ashley Hinson in Iowa, backed Dan Sullivan in Alaska, and held a Republican midterm convention in Dallas. If those candidates were losing ground, the relevant political fact was not that Trump suffered embarrassment. It was that presidential influence had failed to produce public consent.

A verdict, not a humiliation

Calling adverse polling a personal “humiliation” reduces an institutional contest to Trump’s emotional weather. The reported stakes were Senate power, representation, and public judgment about government performance. None of those is clarified by imagining the president embarrassed.

The polling instead suggested a measurable rejection of the governing party’s offer in those states. Respondents reportedly trusted Democrats more on the cost of living, foreign wars, and ordinary people’s interests. Those are assessments of material conditions and governing competence, not merely expressions of distaste for one personality.

The limits of the Trump explanation

AlterNet presents Trump as the common drag on Republican candidates, and the 38 percent approval figure supports that interpretation. But the article also acknowledges that the candidates had distinct weaknesses. It does not establish how much of each polling deficit came from Trump, the nominees, state conditions, or other factors.

That distinction matters because personalization can become a convenient escape hatch for the party around him. Paxton, Hinson, Sullivan, Roger Marshall, Mike Rogers, Jon Husted, and Susan Collins were not passive objects upon whom Trump inflicted polling numbers. They were candidates seeking power under the Republican banner. Their campaigns and records remained their own responsibility.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is a press habit of translating democratic accountability into palace drama. A possible transfer of Senate power becomes a president’s “brutal humiliation”; voters become instruments “taking it out” on his candidates; policy judgments become supporting details in a story about one man’s fortunes.

That framing reverses the hierarchy. Trump’s feelings were politically irrelevant. The consequential actors were voters deciding who would wield legislative authority, and candidates asking to exercise it. Polls could only estimate that decision, not settle it. The systemic error is treating power as personality—and then treating the public’s judgment about power as spectacle.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.
