item.title: 'Rookie mistake' reveals twisted logic fueling DOJ’s 'Loony Tunes' charge
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that the Justice Department filed an “information” accusing former FBI Director James Comey of offenses involving national-defense information—but did not obtain a grand-jury indictment. Former federal prosecutor Andrew Weissmann told The Bulwark’s Sarah Longwell that, because Comey did not consent to waive indictment, the filing does not charge him with a federal felony. Weissmann said the alleged conduct is more than 10 years old and that the applicable statute-o
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Justice Department filed an “information” accusing former FBI Director James Comey of offenses involving national-defense information—but did not obtain a grand-jury indictment. Former federal prosecutor Andrew Weissmann told The Bulwark’s Sarah Longwell that, because Comey did not consent to waive indictment, the filing does not charge him with a federal felony.

Weissmann said the alleged conduct is more than 10 years old and that the applicable statute-of-limitations period may have expired, though he allowed that prosecutors might attempt a short extension. He argued that the legally defective filing nonetheless signals the administration’s desire to pursue Comey, whom Trump associates with the origins of the investigations that shadowed his first presidency.

Power sits with the prosecution

Comey is not the actor exercising state power here. Trump controls the executive branch, and the Justice Department controls federal investigative and prosecutorial machinery. Prosecutors can initiate inquiries, present evidence to grand juries and force targets to spend money defending themselves—even when a charge never survives judicial scrutiny.

That imbalance is the political fact. A failed prosecution is not costless to its target. The process can impose legal bills, reputational damage and years of uncertainty. Weissmann’s account suggests that the filing lacks the grand-jury approval constitutionally required for a felony charge, but its procedural weakness does not erase the coercive authority behind it.

A defective filing still sends a message

According to Weissmann, the filing tells federal law-enforcement personnel that actions perceived as injuring Trump may bring retaliation. That is his interpretation, not a fact independently established by AlterNet. But it fits the reported choice to pursue the most serious version of an allegation at the edge—or possibly beyond the end—of its limitations period.

The crucial decision belongs to Justice Department officials who filed the document without an indictment and despite Comey’s refusal to waive one. Calling that merely a “rookie mistake” risks understating what the reporting describes. Incompetence is one possibility. Another is that the announcement and burden imposed on Comey matter politically even if the case cannot lawfully proceed. The article does not establish which explanation is correct.

The confusion serves the powerful

The distinction between an information and an indictment sounds technical, which makes it useful for political misdirection. Headlines can announce a new “case,” supporters can treat accusation as guilt, and the procedural collapse can arrive later with less attention. The government gains the spectacle of prosecution before proving that it possesses a valid charge.

AlterNet’s framing also wanders through jokes about Comey’s seashell post and comparisons with other Trump controversies. Those details sharpen the absurdity but blur responsibility. The central issue is simpler: the Justice Department reportedly invoked a felony process without securing the grand-jury action required to make that process real.

Punishment without adjudication

No conviction is necessary for prosecution to function as political discipline. The foreseeable costs begin with investigation, public accusation and defense—not with a verdict. When the institution imposing those costs is led by officials aligned with a president’s personal grievances, procedural safeguards become the dividing line between lawful enforcement and personalized state pressure.

Comey’s status as a former FBI director does not make him powerless in ordinary terms. It does make him weaker than the federal government confronting him. Treating the dispute as another round in a feud between famous men obscures the institutional hierarchy: one side has lawyers and a public platform; the other has the machinery of criminal prosecution.

The system can be abused before it succeeds

This episode reveals a broader vulnerability in federal law enforcement. Legal checks may eventually defeat a defective charge, but they do not prevent officials from using an accusation to manufacture suspicion, impose expense or warn other public servants.

The pattern is not simply partisan conflict or bureaucratic confusion. On the facts AlterNet presents, executive power was used to produce the appearance of a felony case without the constitutional step required to create one. A system that measures abuse only by convictions misses the method: power can punish through process, and failure in court may come only after the political objective has already been served.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Fox host issues warning about Trump lies: He’s a 'master media manipulator'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened Fox News veteran Howard Kurtz warned that President Donald Trump’s torrent of false, inflammatory, and trivial remarks is wearing down political journalism. As reported by AlterNet, Kurtz called Trump a “master media manipulator” and argued that reporters increasingly abandon sustained fact-checking because the president produces controversies faster than newsrooms pursue them. Kurtz pointed to Trump’s public claim that he ordered the Justice Department to intervene in an Alaska el
item.content:encoded:
What happened

Fox News veteran Howard Kurtz warned that President Donald Trump’s torrent of false, inflammatory, and trivial remarks is wearing down political journalism. As reported by AlterNet, Kurtz called Trump a “master media manipulator” and argued that reporters increasingly abandon sustained fact-checking because the president produces controversies faster than newsrooms pursue them.

Kurtz pointed to Trump’s public claim that he ordered the Justice Department to intervene in an Alaska election and to what Kurtz described as Trump ordering a raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home near an election. He argued that these consequential stories quickly lost attention to provocative remarks about celebrities, Republican candidates, Norway, and the Nobel Prize.

Kurtz called this failure “Trump Exhaustion Syndrome.” His warning was not that Trump’s conduct is difficult to see, but that journalists repeatedly see it, briefly report it, and then let the next spectacle erase it.

Power is not a personality trait

Trump holds presidential authority. The Justice Department possesses prosecutorial and investigative power. News organizations decide which exercises of that power receive sustained scrutiny and which disappear after a single news cycle.

That hierarchy matters. The central story is not that reporters feel tired or that audiences enjoy vulgar distractions. It is that a president can publicly describe directing federal law enforcement while the institutions responsible for documenting and challenging such conduct move on.

Calling this “exhaustion” risks turning an institutional failure into a medical metaphor. Fatigue does not assign stories, write headlines, reward traffic, or abandon follow-up reporting. Editors and executives make those decisions inside a media economy that prizes immediate attention over accumulated evidence.

The spectacle works because the press rewards it

Kurtz’s examples describe a familiar allocation of attention: a crude or ridiculous remark becomes the irresistible headline, while an assertion of government power receives one burst of coverage and little sustained examination. The trivial material does not merely coexist with the consequential material. It displaces it.

Trump benefits from that imbalance whether every provocation is calculated or, as Kurtz allows, some rally remarks simply run away from him. The observable result is the same: spectacle consumes the limited space that could be used to track official conduct, establish timelines, test claims, and identify who carried out presidential demands.

“Master media manipulator” is therefore only half the diagnosis. Manipulation requires a system willing to be manipulated. Trump supplies the bait; political media repeatedly builds its agenda around it.

The weaker actors are not the cause

Blaming social-media audiences, distracted readers, or an amorphous national attention span lets powerful institutions disappear from their own story. The public does not control newsroom budgets or determine whether a Justice Department intervention receives days of reporting instead of hours.

Kurtz is right to identify the press failure, but “Trump Exhaustion Syndrome” still softens agency. Journalists are not helpless victims of presidential volume. News organizations can distinguish state power from campaign noise. When they decline to do so, they are making an editorial choice with political consequences.

The framing also treats repeated falsehoods as the source of paralysis rather than a reason for more disciplined coverage. If lying becomes so routine that verification is considered pointless, repetition has successfully converted misconduct into background noise.

Normalization is the consequence

The gravest effect is not that any single controversy receives too few clicks. It is that exceptional uses of presidential and prosecutorial power can become ordinary through inadequate follow-up. A boundary does not need to be formally abolished if officials can cross it repeatedly without sustained scrutiny.

Kurtz invokes the historic separation between the White House and Justice Department because that separation restrains presidents from using federal law enforcement as a political instrument. His comparison to how the press might have treated Joe Biden exposes another institutional weakness: conduct is judged not only by what happened, but by how accustomed reporters have become to the person doing it.

That is normalization by attrition. The volume of incidents lowers the perceived importance of each one, even when the cumulative pattern should make the coverage more urgent.

The system learns to look away

This story reveals a political-media structure in which relentless provocation can overwhelm accountability without concealing anything. The conduct happens in public; the failure lies in treating disclosure as resolution.

Trump possesses the government power. Executive officials can enable or resist its use. Media institutions decide whether the public receives a durable record or an endless sequence of disposable outrages. When those institutions describe their retreat as exhaustion, they obscure their own agency.

The systemic error is not simply that spectacle distracts from power. It is that the institutions charged with covering power repeatedly choose the spectacle—and then present their choice as something Trump did to them.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Confusion as Trump abruptly cancels planned rally amid protests, low turnout
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump abruptly canceled a Saturday rally in Kansas, replacing the planned appearance with virtual rallies. The reporting does not establish why he canceled or prove that protests, smaller crowds, or Republican pessimism about the Senate race caused the decision. The event was intended to support Republican Sen. Roger Marshall against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. AlterNet cites a CNN poll showing Hamilton ahead by four points, while not
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump abruptly canceled a Saturday rally in Kansas, replacing the planned appearance with virtual rallies. The reporting does not establish why he canceled or prove that protests, smaller crowds, or Republican pessimism about the Senate race caused the decision.

The event was intended to support Republican Sen. Roger Marshall against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. AlterNet cites a CNN poll showing Hamilton ahead by four points, while noting that Kansas had not elected a Democratic senator since 1939. Commentators speculated that Republicans considered Marshall’s race a lost cause, but the article provides no confirmation from Trump’s campaign or the GOP.

Trump’s previous Kansas appearance was interrupted by protesters, at least 11 of whom were escorted out, according to the Independent. Trump called protesters “paid” without evidence and used an antisemitic slur while defending Marshall’s record of suing former patients over medical debt. AlterNet also reports noticeably smaller venues and crowds at other recent Trump events.

The unanswered question

The headline offers protests and low turnout as an explanation. The reporting offers only proximity: protests happened, crowds elsewhere appeared smaller, and then Trump canceled Kansas.

That may justify scrutiny, but it does not establish causation. A sharper account would separate what the campaign decided from what commentators guessed. Here, the central decision-maker is clear; the rationale is not.

Power canceled the rally

This was not merely “confusion.” Trump held the power to appear, withdraw, or redirect his campaign operation toward virtual events. Marshall, despite being the incumbent senator the rally was supposed to assist, was left to absorb the political consequence.

The institutional stakes extend beyond Trump’s travel schedule. Republicans were defending a Senate seat in a state where their party had maintained an extraordinary historical advantage. If the campaign judged the race unrecoverable, cancellation would be resource allocation by the party’s dominant figure—not an atmospheric mystery created by protesters.

Protesters became the decoy

The weaker actors in this story are the people removed from political events. They did not control the venue, the campaign calendar, or the Senate strategy. Yet Trump reportedly answered their dissent by calling them “paid,” including at the South Carolina rally where the Kansas cancellation was announced.

That unsupported label performs a familiar propaganda function: it converts visible opposition into a supposedly artificial conspiracy. The claim avoids confronting the substance of dissent and encourages supporters to treat disapproval as fraudulent by definition.

The conduct matters more than the crowd

Shrinking venues and an attendee’s Jonestown comparison made vivid television, but spectacle can obscure the more consequential conduct. At the earlier Kansas event, Trump used an antisemitic slur while defending Marshall’s lawsuits against former patients over unpaid medical bills.

Crowd size measures political energy imperfectly. A president normalizing a slur from the stage is an exercise of power in public: it signals what language the movement will tolerate and what behavior its leaders will excuse. Treating that episode as another colorful detail understates its significance.

The system behind the mystery

This story reveals how personality-driven politics distorts campaign reporting. A president makes an unexplained decision; journalists and commentators search protests, polling, and crowd shots for clues; the decision itself remains insulated from accountability because the person with the answer does not provide one.

The result is coverage built around speculation about optics while power escapes examination. Protesters become possible culprits, dwindling crowds become the drama, and the central fact recedes: Trump’s campaign canceled support for a vulnerable incumbent and did not publicly supply the reason. When political leaders withhold explanations, the press should identify that evasion plainly—not convert it into fog.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

item.title: Leak: Trump personally directing plot to challenge election results
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, citing reporting by Zeteo, says President Donald Trump was personally directing a White House and Republican effort to prepare challenges to the approaching midterm elections. A Trump adviser told Zeteo that “the president and the White House” were steering the campaign, which included Justice Department litigation, claims about noncitizen voting, pressure on election officials, and preparations for disputes over results. Zeteo reported that Trump publicly took responsibi
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, citing reporting by Zeteo, says President Donald Trump was personally directing a White House and Republican effort to prepare challenges to the approaching midterm elections. A Trump adviser told Zeteo that “the president and the White House” were steering the campaign, which included Justice Department litigation, claims about noncitizen voting, pressure on election officials, and preparations for disputes over results.

Zeteo reported that Trump publicly took responsibility for a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to invalidate the result of an Alaska Senate race if the Republican candidate did not win. The outlet also described officials as concerned about possible federal deployments at polling places, seizures of election equipment, and attempts to obstruct certification. Those were reported as feared scenarios, not completed actions, and Trump had declined to rule them out.

The Justice Department did not answer Zeteo’s questions, including whether its public-integrity leadership had waived internal guidelines against interfering with state election administration. The reporting therefore establishes an organized pressure campaign and an extraordinary conditional lawsuit, but not that every contemplated measure would occur.

The power is federal

This is not primarily a story about partisan operatives trading inflammatory claims. The institutional power described belongs to the president, the White House, and a Justice Department capable of making arrests, bringing prosecutions, filing lawsuits, and forcing state officials to defend their election systems in court.

Trump is not depicted as a spectator being manipulated by reckless subordinates. Zeteo’s sources identify him as the person issuing directions, while his own statement—“I’m the one that said do it”—ties him directly to the Alaska litigation. The chain of agency runs upward, not downward.

Legitimacy made conditional

The Alaska case, as described, contains the core abuse: an election result would be treated as legally suspect depending on which party won. That is not election integrity. It is an attempt to make Republican victory the test of electoral validity.

The lawsuits need not succeed to produce damage. Federal litigation can burden state administrators, amplify unsupported suspicions, and prepare supporters to interpret defeat as proof of fraud. The practical objective inferred from this conduct is not merely to win a case; it is to establish a political permission structure for rejecting unwanted outcomes.

Fear is part of the machinery

Claims about noncitizen voting supply the pretext. Arrests, prosecution threats, and federal intervention supply the coercive capacity. Together they shift election administration from a rules-based process into a test of whether state and local officials can withstand pressure from the executive branch.

Coverage can misdirect responsibility when it presents election officials as simply anxious about an uncertain season. Their anxiety is not the cause of the crisis. According to Zeteo, officials were responding to specific possibilities raised or left open by the president and to actions already taken by his administration. Calling that atmosphere “confusion” would conceal who created it.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is the conversion of state power into a partisan contingency plan: courts to precondition legitimacy, prosecutors to intimidate administrators, federal personnel as a possible presence around voting, and presidential rhetoric to prime rejection of defeat.

The unresolved question is how far the administration would go, not who possessed the authority to escalate. Zeteo’s reporting places that authority—and the direction behind its use—inside the White House. A political system fails long before ballots are physically seized if it accepts the premise that election law binds the government only when the government likes the result.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump pays the price for ditching the message that put him in power
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump has lost support among parts of his political base because he has drifted from the populist, working-class message that helped elect him. Summarizing Politico columnist Alexander Burns, the article says Trump has emphasized attacks on Democrats while failing to address cost-of-living concerns with a clear, consistent message. Burns also attributes some MAGA dissatisfaction to the war in Iran and contrasts Trump’s scattered approach with
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump has lost support among parts of his political base because he has drifted from the populist, working-class message that helped elect him. Summarizing Politico columnist Alexander Burns, the article says Trump has emphasized attacks on Democrats while failing to address cost-of-living concerns with a clear, consistent message.

Burns also attributes some MAGA dissatisfaction to the war in Iran and contrasts Trump’s scattered approach with the political discipline of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The report says polls and early forecasts indicate declining popular support and growing interest in change before the midterm elections, but it supplies no figures establishing the size or durability of that movement.

Power is not messaging

The article treats Trump’s problem principally as a failure of communication. That framing is convenient because it turns governing into branding: if voters are anxious about prices, the president supposedly needs a better sentence about prices.

But Trump holds presidential power. The relevant question is not merely whether he can recover the language of economic populism. It is what his administration has done with its authority—and whether those decisions have improved the material conditions he once promised to change. A president is not a commentator trapped behind an ineffective slogan.

The base is not in charge

Former supporters can withdraw approval, punish candidates in primaries, or stay home. They cannot direct foreign policy, set executive priorities, or make the administration confront living costs. Trump and the officials around him possess that agency.

Blaming his weakening position on a “scattered campaign strategy” risks shifting responsibility from the powerful actor making decisions to the audience refusing to applaud them. Voter discontent is not a communications malfunction. It is one of the few remaining checks available to people who were promised attention and now believe they are not receiving it.

Authoritarianism as campaign advice

The comparisons with Lula and Netanyahu flatten radically different political methods into a lesson about message discipline. Most troubling is the treatment of Netanyahu’s fear-based appeals—casting opponents as weak on Iran and Arab parties as an internal menace—as an effective template for retaining power.

That may describe a political tactic, but presenting scapegoating and militarized fear chiefly as smart electoral positioning sanitizes their consequences. According to the account, Netanyahu also sought further strikes on Iran before an election. The story does not establish his motive, so it cannot be called an electoral maneuver as fact. Even so, war policy and the depiction of minorities as internal threats deserve scrutiny as exercises of state power, not admiration as campaign craftsmanship.

The comforting misdirection

Burns’s warning that Trump could recover by returning to populism is plausible within the article’s evidence, but it exposes the weakness of the analysis. It assumes the decisive variable is whether Trump can sound like the candidate voters remember.

That lets political institutions disappear behind rhetoric. Congress, executive agencies, party organizations, major donors, and the presidency itself become scenery while “the message” does all the causal work. The result is horse-race coverage that measures whether power can reproduce itself without examining how that power has been used.

A system that grades the sales pitch

The larger pattern is a political press more comfortable evaluating persuasion than accountability. Leaders are judged on whether they soothe, frighten, or mobilize the correct constituency—not on the governing choices producing insecurity, alienation, or war.

Trump’s reported decline may be temporary; the article offers no basis for declaring otherwise. But if his standing recovers after another populist pivot, that will not prove the underlying grievances were addressed. It will show how easily political analysis confuses renewed loyalty to a leader with material relief for the people he governs.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: The crack in MAGA's armor —and why Americans are turning on Trump
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, summarizing Atlantic writer David A. Graham, reports that recent Fox News, CNBC, and Financial Times polling found government corruption rivaling or surpassing economic concerns among voters. The Financial Times survey reportedly found about 69 percent of registered voters—and nearly half of Trump’s 2024 voters—concerned about corruption, self-dealing, or conflicts of interest in the Trump White House. Graham argues that no single scandal caused this shift. Instead, the p
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, summarizing Atlantic writer David A. Graham, reports that recent Fox News, CNBC, and Financial Times polling found government corruption rivaling or surpassing economic concerns among voters. The Financial Times survey reportedly found about 69 percent of registered voters—and nearly half of Trump’s 2024 voters—concerned about corruption, self-dealing, or conflicts of interest in the Trump White House.

Graham argues that no single scandal caused this shift. Instead, the polls and Trump’s declining favorability suggest a cumulative loss of confidence. He points to questions surrounding Trump family business interests, privately funded White House projects, data-center promotion, and foreign policy involving Ukraine, Iran, Russia, and Middle Eastern governments. The article supplies critics’ arguments about those connections, not evidence establishing that business interests dictated policy.

The power is in the presidency

The decisive actor here is not an abstract “MAGA movement,” much less a surprised electorate. Trump holds the presidency. His administration controls executive policy, while the president’s family businesses create the conflicts that voters are reportedly noticing.

That distinction matters because “corruption” can become a foggy label detached from conduct. The institutional issue is concrete: presidential authority can affect regulation, procurement, diplomacy, and war, while private interests linked to the president’s family may benefit from access or policy. The reporting raises that concern but does not prove every alleged connection.

Accumulation finally has a political cost

The headline promises a single crack in Trump’s political armor. The reporting describes something less cinematic and more consequential: voters may be registering the accumulated weight of recurring conflicts rather than reacting to one definitive revelation.

That is how normalized misconduct often becomes politically legible. Each controversy is treated as an isolated story, burdened with its own evidentiary disputes and quickly displaced by the next. The public eventually sees the pattern that episodic coverage obscures: public power repeatedly operating beside private enrichment and undisclosed influence.

Polling is evidence, not a verdict

AlterNet overstates what these surveys establish when it declares that Americans are “turning on Trump.” The reported polls show heightened concern about corruption. They do not, by themselves, prove why opinions changed, predict an election, or demonstrate that every respondent understands corruption in the same way.

Nor does declining favorability establish a single cause. Graham’s cumulative explanation is plausible, but it remains an interpretation. Strong political analysis does not need to inflate polling into certainty; the reported concern is striking enough without pretending it settles voter behavior.

Congress chose much of this weakness

The story ends by imagining a future House majority investigating Trump administration conduct. That correctly identifies congressional oversight as a source of real power, but it also exposes the existing institutional failure.

Presidential conflicts persist not merely because voters have been inattentive, but because lawmakers can decline to investigate, narrow inquiries, or treat oversight as partisan theater. A House majority could issue subpoenas and examine whether official decisions intersected with private interests. Until it does, “concern” remains a polling result while executive power continues operating.

The system rewards scandal without resolution

The larger pattern is not that economics suddenly stopped mattering. It is that corruption and household costs are not cleanly separable when public decisions can enrich insiders, privilege donors, or redirect national policy without transparent justification.

The political system repeatedly converts conflicts of interest into media controversy, then waits for voters to impose consequences that institutions refused to pursue. That is the misdirection at the center of the story: accountability is framed as a change in public mood when the officials holding investigative and legislative power have had agency all along.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: 'Off the deep end': Alarm bells ring over 'bizarre' new Trump campaign spree
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that author Jennifer Welch called President Donald Trump’s recent campaign appearances “bizarre” and “unacceptable,” citing strange noises, forgotten names, comments about male politicians’ bodies, and public mockery of Republican allies. The supposed “alarm bells” in the headline refer chiefly to Welch’s commentary, not to a newly reported medical finding or organized warning from multiple experts. Welch highlighted Trump’s praise of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s backsid
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that author Jennifer Welch called President Donald Trump’s recent campaign appearances “bizarre” and “unacceptable,” citing strange noises, forgotten names, comments about male politicians’ bodies, and public mockery of Republican allies. The supposed “alarm bells” in the headline refer chiefly to Welch’s commentary, not to a newly reported medical finding or organized warning from multiple experts.

Welch highlighted Trump’s praise of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s backside, his insult about Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s appearance, and his ridicule of Sen. Ted Cruz while discussing a hypothetical Supreme Court appointment. AlterNet also cites psychologist Alan D. Blotcky, who told the outlet earlier in October that, in his opinion, Trump acts nihilistically and cares primarily about chaos, personal acclaim, and financial gain.

The power is not diagnostic

The consequential fact is not whether commentators can assign Trump a psychological label from afar. It is that the president used campaign appearances to objectify, insult, and humiliate political allies—and those allies remained publicly accommodating.

Trump held the institutional power in every encounter described. Husted, Paxton, and Cruz were not helpless citizens confronting an erratic stranger. They were Republican officials operating inside a political structure dominated by a president whose approval, endorsements, and retaliation could affect their careers.

Submission as political theater

Welch’s strongest observation concerns the men who “race up” to accept humiliation or objectification. Cruz’s reported response is especially revealing: Trump said Democrats and Republicans alike hated him, and Cruz stood, smiled, and waved.

That exchange does not establish Trump’s mental condition. It does demonstrate a hierarchy. The leader dispenses ridicule; the subordinate converts degradation into loyalty theater. What looks merely strange at the level of personality becomes politically legible once power enters the frame.

A headline stronger than its evidence

AlterNet packages the episode as experts sounding alarms over a campaign “spree,” but the article supplies one author’s podcast commentary and one psychologist’s sweeping opinion from an earlier interview. It provides no clinical evaluation, no response from Trump or the officials discussed, and no evidence establishing Blotcky’s claims about Trump’s ultimate intentions or finances.

That weakness matters. Speculation about whether Trump is “off the deep end” shifts attention from conduct the reporting actually describes to a diagnosis it cannot establish. The behavior does not need amateur medical certification to warrant scrutiny. Public humiliation, personal fixation, and enforced deference are political facts when practiced by the person who controls the executive branch and dominates his party.

The pattern beneath the spectacle

The familiar misdirection is to treat Trump’s conduct as a puzzle of temperament while Republican compliance becomes background scenery. That framing turns a power arrangement into a personality story.

The larger pattern is institutional submission: elected officials accept insult because proximity to presidential power remains more valuable than dignity or independence. The bizarre remarks attract attention, but the consequential event is the room’s response. A political system degrades when powerful people learn that smiling through humiliation is the price of access—and decide the price is worth paying.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump was warned of alleged China spy’s ties to CEO donor — and did nothing
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, summarizing New York Times reporting, says U.S. intelligence officials concluded that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing ties to Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. The reporting does not identify what information she allegedly passed, and China’s embassy called the allegations groundless. The concern reached the White House, but the supplied reporting does not establish that Donald Tru
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, summarizing New York Times reporting, says U.S. intelligence officials concluded that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing ties to Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. The reporting does not identify what information she allegedly passed, and China’s embassy called the allegations groundless.

The concern reached the White House, but the supplied reporting does not establish that Donald Trump personally received a warning or made a specific decision to disregard one. It says Jensen Huang was not given a defensive briefing; officials may have withheld one to protect continuing surveillance, though the Times could not confirm that explanation.

Nvidia denied wrongdoing and said Megaspeed received no sensitive trade secrets or national-security information. Megaspeed said it would cooperate with U.S. authorities. A Commerce Department investigation begun in late 2024 was transferred to the Justice Department in 2026.

The headline outruns the evidence

The headline assigns Trump direct knowledge and direct inaction. The article body establishes something narrower: intelligence agencies raised alarms, the White House knew of the concern, and the government did not warn Jensen Huang. It does not document what Trump was told, when he was told, or what options officials presented to him.

That gap matters. Trump’s administration deserves scrutiny because executive power ultimately sits above the agencies managing export controls, intelligence risks, and defensive briefings. But accountability becomes weaker, not stronger, when a headline claims a documented presidential choice that the underlying reporting does not actually show.

Power sat in Washington

Alice Huang’s alleged conduct is the counterintelligence concern, but she did not control American safeguards. Federal officials controlled surveillance, briefings, export policy, investigations, and enforcement. The administration controlled whether commercial access to China would be restricted or expanded.

Those officials apparently faced a genuine operational tradeoff: warning Jensen Huang might have protected him while jeopardizing surveillance. Yet the reporting cannot determine whether that tradeoff explains the silence. “Nobody warned him” is an outcome; it is not, by itself, proof of why the government chose it.

Money and access complicate policy

Jensen Huang was not merely another executive seeking regulatory relief. According to the Times account, he had become an influential Trump ally, successfully pressed the president to retreat from restrictions on chip sales to China, and Nvidia contributed $20 million toward Trump’s ballroom.

Those facts do not prove a corrupt bargain, nor do they establish that Nvidia knew of espionage or chip smuggling. They do expose a structural conflict: a company with enormous financial stakes in China gained privileged political access while national-security officials were reportedly investigating whether safeguards around advanced chips had been breached.

The decisive imbalance is not between one suspected intelligence asset and one supposedly unsuspecting executive. It is between public institutions charged with protecting strategically important technology and a corporate actor wealthy enough to shape the policy governing that technology.

The unanswered decision

The central question is who allowed commercial and diplomatic priorities to override—or coexist uneasily with—counterintelligence warnings. The supplied reporting does not answer it. It identifies surveillance, an unissued briefing, lobbying success, a large contribution, and an investigation changing hands. It does not connect those facts with evidence of a presidential order or a knowing corporate violation.

That uncertainty should direct further scrutiny upward, toward named decision-makers at the White House, Commerce Department, Justice Department, and intelligence agencies. Instead, the framing offers a more dramatic but less substantiated story about Trump personally doing nothing, while the bureaucratic chain of responsibility remains obscure.

A system built for influence

This episode reveals how national-security policy becomes vulnerable when enforcement decisions share a corridor with donor access and corporate lobbying. No secret agreement is required. Concentrated wealth can secure meetings, shape exceptions, and make aggressive enforcement politically costly, while officials hide consequential choices behind classified processes and institutional ambiguity.

The result is a system in which the government can invoke technological competition with China, corporations can pursue the Chinese market, and responsibility for failed safeguards can remain permanently unresolved. The alleged spy is the easiest figure to condemn. The harder problem is an American power structure that leaves the public unable to determine who made the decisions that mattered.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: 'Worried' former Trump aide drops a bomb on GOP's future
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that former Trump communications director Bryan Lanza warned the Republican Party could lose a U.S. Senate seat in Texas and expressed concern about Republican candidates in Mississippi and Kansas. His “bomb” was not a new disclosure, but a bleak electoral assessment: he said he would not be surprised to see Republicans lose Texas when results arrived the following Wednesday. Speaking with CNN’s Jake Tapper on the Thursday before the election, Lanza blamed the Texa
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former Trump communications director Bryan Lanza warned the Republican Party could lose a U.S. Senate seat in Texas and expressed concern about Republican candidates in Mississippi and Kansas. His “bomb” was not a new disclosure, but a bleak electoral assessment: he said he would not be surprised to see Republicans lose Texas when results arrived the following Wednesday.

Speaking with CNN’s Jake Tapper on the Thursday before the election, Lanza blamed the Texas danger on Republicans replacing Senator John Cornyn with Ken Paxton, whose record had become the focus of a damaging advertisement. In the ad, several Texas Republicans supporting the Democratic candidate called Paxton corrupt and cited his legal troubles and impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House.

AlterNet also notes that former Paxton aides accused him of bribery and abuse of office, allegations Paxton disputed through what the whistleblowers described as false or misleading campaign statements. The Texas Senate’s Republican majority ultimately spared him removal after his impeachment. Lanza estimated Republican spending across the contested races could approach $500 million, while reporting weak enthusiasm in Mississippi and Kansas.

The warning is about losing, not wrongdoing

Lanza’s anxiety is revealingly narrow. His complaint is not that Republican institutions tolerated a candidate burdened by serious allegations and an impeachment. It is that the candidate might cost the party a seat.

That distinction matters. Paxton’s record was not hidden from Republican officials. According to AlterNet, whistleblowers had spoken publicly about their accusations as far back as 2022, and the Texas House later impeached him. Republican senators nevertheless preserved his political career. The party’s problem, as Lanza describes it, began when voters might impose a consequence that Republican officeholders declined to impose themselves.

Even his praise for Cornyn is managerial: Cornyn would have “run away” with the race, generated enthusiasm and avoided enormous spending. Electoral efficiency substitutes for institutional accountability.

Republicans held the power

The weaker actors here were not the people controlling the outcome. Whistleblowers could make allegations. Former Republican officials could appear in an advertisement. Voters could react. But Texas Republicans possessed the institutional power to decide whether impeachment would remove Paxton, and the Senate majority spared him.

That makes the party’s current predicament an internally produced result. Republican officials enabled Paxton’s survival; Republican voters then selected him over Cornyn, as Lanza’s remarks indicate; Republican organizations were left financing the consequences. Treating the resulting contest as an ominous “specter” obscures the chain of agency.

The corruption allegations did not simply descend on the GOP. Its own governing machinery confronted them and declined to end Paxton’s career.

A headline inflates an admission

Calling Lanza’s remarks a “bomb” oversells what is essentially a strategist acknowledging visible electoral damage. He revealed no concealed misconduct and offered no new evidence against Paxton. He admitted that Republicans might lose races they expected to control.

That framing makes insider nervousness the dramatic center of the story, when the more consequential fact is institutional protection. The powerful become worried spectators in a crisis their party helped create, while “corruption” is described almost like bad weather haunting them.

The language also risks collapsing distinct claims. Republican critics called Paxton corrupt; former aides accused him of bribery and abuse of office; the Texas House impeached him; the Senate did not remove him. Those facts establish a serious record of allegations and political proceedings, not every accusation as a proven criminal finding.

Accountability reduced to scheduling

Lanza’s closing reassurance exposes the operative ethic: after Election Day, Republicans would begin planning the next election. Defeat, if it came, would be processed as a tactical setback rather than evidence of institutional failure.

That is the larger pattern. Parties often protect powerful figures while accountability remains an internal choice, then rediscover concern when the liability reaches polling, fundraising or seat counts. Conduct that failed to trigger decisive action suddenly becomes urgent once it threatens control.

The system does not lack information. It lacks incentives for governing institutions to act before misconduct allegations become expensive. Under that arrangement, accountability is not a standard applied by those with power. It is a cost imposed later—if voters can still make it stick.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump’s next golf makeover comes with Superfund toxic sludge
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened President Donald Trump waived certain state and federal water-pollution requirements in June for a proposed renovation of the golf complex at Joint Base Andrews, invoking “national security,” according to AlterNet’s account of Politico’s reporting. Parts of the Maryland complex sit above a landfill within a Superfund site contaminated with heavy metals, polychlorinated biphenyls and “forever chemicals.” Jack Nicklaus’s firm is slated to oversee the redesign. Maryland Environment Se
item.content:encoded:
What happened

President Donald Trump waived certain state and federal water-pollution requirements in June for a proposed renovation of the golf complex at Joint Base Andrews, invoking “national security,” according to AlterNet’s account of Politico’s reporting. Parts of the Maryland complex sit above a landfill within a Superfund site contaminated with heavy metals, polychlorinated biphenyls and “forever chemicals.” Jack Nicklaus’s firm is slated to oversee the redesign.

Maryland Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain said state inspectors were denied access and warned that the Air Force had neither sought wetlands permits nor completed applications covering erosion and stormwater runoff. Joint Base Andrews disputed her account of the inspection, while the Air Force said any future work would avoid contaminated soil and comply with applicable environmental laws. The unresolved questions are whether construction could spread pollution into neighboring properties and whether Maryland retains meaningful oversight after Trump’s waiver.

Power wears a security badge

The decisive actor is not Maryland, nearby residents or military families. It is the president, exercising federal authority over a military installation and using that authority to change which environmental safeguards constrain the project.

“National security” ordinarily describes protection against an identifiable danger. Here, the administration applied it to renovating golf courses. The White House offered no security rationale in the reporting beyond the designation itself; instead, its statement praised Trump’s golfing ability and “eye for detail and design.” That is marketing language for a discretionary amenity, not an explanation of military necessity.

The label matters because it converts a personal design preference into an assertion of institutional urgency. Once that happens, ordinary permitting and scrutiny can be treated as obstacles rather than protections.

The contamination is not the controversy

A golf course atop a contaminated site is not inherently extraordinary. As former EPA official Clifford Villa explained, such a use can help cap polluted ground. The political issue is whether renovation will disturb that containment or allow contaminated runoff to travel beyond it.

The Air Force says it will avoid known contamination, stay away from the creek and follow applicable law. Maryland officials say required applications remain incomplete and construction could begin before approvals arrive. Those positions cannot be reconciled through assurances alone. Inspection, testing and enforceable conditions exist because the institution conducting the work has an interest in declaring its own precautions sufficient.

That makes the dispute over inspector access especially important. McIlwain says inspectors were denied entry; the base says an inspector was escorted onto the installation. The reporting does not resolve the contradiction. But a regulator’s ability to inspect cannot depend on the regulated institution’s preferred account of its own conduct.

Risk pushed downhill

If the Air Force’s assurances prove wrong, the consequences will not fall primarily on the officials who approved the project. They could reach neighbors through runoff, while service members and their families inherit a renovated facility built under weakened scrutiny.

That is the familiar distribution of power: federal officials claim discretion, contractors receive the work, and people living near the site absorb the uncertainty. The administration presents future enjoyment as the benefit while treating environmental oversight as negotiable—even though the potential harm extends beyond the course boundary.

The weaker actors are therefore positioned to prove danger before construction, while the government controlling the site asks them to trust promises it has made harder to examine.

A makeover disguised as necessity

The article’s celebrity-golf framing risks making the story sound like another episode in Trump’s fixation on aesthetics. His preferences are relevant: AlterNet reports no public record that he has played the Andrews course, yet he criticized it, toured it from the air with Nicklaus and installed Nicklaus’s firm as designer.

But taste is not the central abuse of power here. The consequential decision was using presidential authority to waive pollution requirements for a discretionary renovation on contaminated federal land. The question is not whether Trump can recognize a good golf course. It is why that claim should carry any weight against unfinished permits, contested inspection access and a Superfund site’s documented hazards.

Exception becomes government

This episode shows how executive power expands through mundane projects. A waiver does not need tanks in the street to matter. It can operate through paperwork, restricted access and a phrase broad enough to convert an amenity into a security project.

The larger pattern is government by exception: declare an ordinary presidential preference extraordinary, reduce outside oversight, and leave subordinate agencies to promise that everything will still be handled responsibly. The public is then asked to judge safety from statements issued by the same institutions that displaced the safeguards meant to establish it.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: GOP lawmaker humiliated live on CNN as Kaitlan Collins exposes epic blunder
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Texas Republican Rep. Chip Roy’s “epic blunder” was repeatedly telling CNN’s Kaitlan Collins that Republicans should be allowed to “finish the job”—the slogan closely associated with Joe Biden’s abandoned reelection campaign. Collins pointed out the overlap, briefly leaving Roy without an answer. Roy was arguing that Republicans deserved two more years to lower prices, interest rates and inflation. Collins noted that Donald Trump had already campaigned on redu
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Texas Republican Rep. Chip Roy’s “epic blunder” was repeatedly telling CNN’s Kaitlan Collins that Republicans should be allowed to “finish the job”—the slogan closely associated with Joe Biden’s abandoned reelection campaign. Collins pointed out the overlap, briefly leaving Roy without an answer.

Roy was arguing that Republicans deserved two more years to lower prices, interest rates and inflation. Collins noted that Donald Trump had already campaigned on reducing living costs in 2024. She also challenged Roy over Trump’s praise for oil-company profits while AAA put regular gasoline at about $4.23 a gallon that Thursday, up from roughly $3.04 a year earlier.

The interview exposed another evasion when Roy would not say whether Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton was running a good Senate campaign. Collins emphasized that he had declined to answer. Roy, who lost a Republican primary for Texas attorney general earlier in the year, is leaving Congress when his term ends.

The slogan is not the failure

Borrowing Biden’s line was embarrassing, but it was not the consequential mistake. The larger problem was Roy’s admission that Republicans were still asking voters to wait for the affordability gains Trump had already promised.

That is what Collins’s first interruption established. Roy presented cheaper food, housing and fuel as the next Republican offer. Collins reminded him that it was also the previous one. The slogan became viral bait because television prefers a clean partisan gaffe to a harder question: who has governing power, and what has that power produced?

Power cannot run as an outsider

Trump controls the executive branch. Roy holds federal legislative power. Neither is merely an observer advising some distant government to act.

Yet Roy’s pitch converted responsibility into an extension request. Republicans had “only” had 21 months, he argued, while citing spending, taxes, government employment and border security as evidence of progress. That defense quietly changed the standard. The promised result was lower living costs; the substitute evidence was a list of ideological priorities.

Voters paying more for gasoline cannot purchase groceries with reduced government headcount. If those policies have not delivered the advertised relief, reciting them does not close the gap. It identifies it.

The public gets excuses, capital gets praise

Collins’s question about oil-company profits reached the actual distribution of power. Drivers faced higher pump prices while Trump, according to AlterNet, praised the money major oil companies were making. Roy answered that Trump had previously criticized companies for not passing gains to consumers.

That is not an account of enforcement, legislation or material leverage. It is another statement about what Trump said. The administration can shape energy policy, federal regulation and the government’s response to the conflict with Iran. Roy can legislate and conduct oversight. Asking corporations to share their gains is rhetoric offered in place of an identified mechanism.

Roy blamed the unfinished work on insufficient time while also asking voters to credit the same officials for progress. Power claims authorship when the numbers are useful and discovers complexity when prices rise.

Evasion is also an answer

Roy’s refusal to assess Paxton’s campaign was not a policy dispute, but it exposed the same political discipline. A direct judgment could create a cost inside Republican politics, so Roy withheld it. Collins did not need to manufacture a confession; she simply repeated the unanswered question.

That matters because institutional cowardice often appears as conversational fog. Politicians answer the question that protects their alliances, then rely on the interview’s momentum to conceal the substitution. Collins stopped the momentum. Roy’s silence supplied the information he would not state.

The governing pattern

The Biden slogan made the segment memorable, but the deeper continuity is more damaging: officials in power campaign as though delivery is always one election away. Every failure becomes unfinished business; every measurable hardship becomes a messaging challenge.

The institutional imbalance is plain. The White House and members of Congress possess tools that consumers do not. Oil companies possess pricing power that drivers do not. Yet the burden is shifted downward, onto voters asked to provide more patience while officeholders offer promises recycled from the politicians they defeated.

The systemic error is not that Roy used the wrong slogan. It is that the political class keeps treating accountability as a branding problem—and television too often agrees, unless an interviewer insists on returning to the question.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Gloves off: Warning Trump’s second term is about to get way more tumultuous
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened The warning is that President Donald Trump may intensify tariffs and military pressure on Iran after the midterm elections. AlterNet, summarizing Politico, reports that Republican officials, industry representatives, congressional aides, and current and former officials expect a more volatile second half of Trump’s term, including potentially higher tariffs. Politico reported that Trump wanted tariffs restored near levels preceding a February Supreme Court ruling that invalidated m
item.content:encoded:
What happened

The warning is that President Donald Trump may intensify tariffs and military pressure on Iran after the midterm elections. AlterNet, summarizing Politico, reports that Republican officials, industry representatives, congressional aides, and current and former officials expect a more volatile second half of Trump’s term, including potentially higher tariffs.

Politico reported that Trump wanted tariffs restored near levels preceding a February Supreme Court ruling that invalidated many of them. It also reported that new trade measures were being prepared, the Pentagon was sending additional forces to the Middle East, and Trump had suggested further action involving Iran.

A White House official called discussion of future tariff rates “baseless speculation” and said announcements would come from the administration. According to Politico, the White House did not answer separate questions about its post-midterm Iran plans. The reporting therefore establishes preparations and expectations—not a confirmed post-election decision.

The power is in the White House

Trump holds the decisive institutional power described here. His administration can initiate trade measures, direct foreign policy, and deploy military resources, subject to legal and congressional constraints. Consumers, border-state businesses, and Republican candidates can absorb the consequences, but they do not control those decisions.

That distinction matters because the story’s anonymous voices describe turmoil as though it were approaching like weather. It is not weather. Any new duties would be imposed by the administration. Any further military action would result from choices made by officials empowered to order it.

Republicans want distance, not restraint

The reported Republican response is political self-preservation. Candidates in competitive races, including in Michigan, sought distance from tariffs affecting trade with Canada. One Michigan Republican said the tariffs were “hammering us,” while a House Republican argued that Midwestern candidates might win despite them.

But distancing rhetoric is not institutional opposition. The article provides no evidence that these Republicans successfully constrained Trump’s tariff policy or the reported military buildup. Their objection, as presented, is largely that the policies could cost Republicans elections—not that imposing broad costs by executive choice is itself an abuse of power.

Unpredictability is a misleading frame

Calling the prospective agenda “tumultuous” or “unpredictable” obscures what the reporting actually describes: identifiable officials considering identifiable actions with foreseeable economic effects. Higher tariffs can raise costs for importers and consumers. Escalation involving Iran can push oil and gasoline prices upward and expose people to far graver consequences than electoral discomfort.

The precise scale of those effects remains uncertain, and the article does not establish that every price increase it mentions resulted solely from Trump’s decisions. But uncertainty about magnitude is not confusion about agency. The administration would own the choice to escalate.

Elections as temporary discipline

The most revealing allegation is that electoral pressure moderated Trump before the midterms and that its removal could free him to act more aggressively afterward. Politico’s sources did not describe a president reconsidering policy after evidence of public harm. They described one potentially delaying or softening action to protect congressional majorities.

That interpretation remains a forecast from unnamed and interested sources, not a proven account of Trump’s motives. Still, it exposes the governing culture surrounding him: Republican and industry insiders apparently regard public accountability as a temporary tactical constraint rather than a reason to change course.

The system rewards evasion

The larger pattern is executive power paired with partisan cowardice. The White House retains room to act, congressional Republicans complain when consequences reach their districts, and anonymous insiders translate deliberate policy choices into warnings about volatility.

That arrangement lets powerful actors evade responsibility at every stage. The administration can dismiss advance reporting as speculation. Republican candidates can posture as bystanders. Industry officials can predict damage without attaching their names. Then consumers and communities are left to experience political decisions as an inexplicable crisis instead of the foreseeable product of who held power, what they chose, and who declined to stop them.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Damning supercut of corruption features all the grifting in Trumpworld
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Jonathan V. Last and Catherine Rampell used a Friday episode of The Bulwark’s “Receipts” to survey alleged self-dealing and influence-peddling among people in Donald Trump’s orbit. Their central argument was that Trumpworld does not punish grifting as such; it punishes grifting that proceeds without Trump’s approval or benefit. The discussion centered on a New York Times report that Justice Department official Alina Habba Mildon allegedly signed a $50 million
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Jonathan V. Last and Catherine Rampell used a Friday episode of The Bulwark’s “Receipts” to survey alleged self-dealing and influence-peddling among people in Donald Trump’s orbit. Their central argument was that Trumpworld does not punish grifting as such; it punishes grifting that proceeds without Trump’s approval or benefit.

The discussion centered on a New York Times report that Justice Department official Alina Habba Mildon allegedly signed a $50 million general-counsel contract with a company founded by the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini while Herrera was seeking a presidential pardon. According to AlterNet’s account, the family paid $10 million before Trump, angered by the arrangement, said it should pay no more. Last and Rampell also discussed allegations or reporting involving Kristi Noem, Corey Lewandowski, Kimberly Guilfoyle, James Blair, Chris LaCivita and Brad Parscale. The supplied report does not establish criminal liability or independently resolve every allegation it repeats.

The power sits at the top

The decisive fact is not that political operatives pursued money. It is that Trump reportedly possessed the power to bless the arrangement, condemn it and communicate that the remaining payment should stop. Habba Mildon may have negotiated the contract, and the family may have agreed to it, but the president controlled the asset the family reportedly wanted: a pardon.

That distinction exposes the structure. Access to sovereign power becomes commercially valuable when people close to its holder can plausibly sell influence over it. The problem is larger than whether Trump personally received a “cut,” as Last joked. A presidency organized around personal permission turns public authority into a market controlled by the ruler and his circle.

Corruption is not a comedy genre

Last and Rampell describe the conduct through mob-film jokes and images of bumbling imitators. The ridicule is understandable, but it can also shrink the scandal. Incompetence does not neutralize influence trading. Clumsy actors can still redirect public money, exploit official access and make government decisions answerable to private relationships.

The alleged effort by Lewandowski to avoid putting a threat in writing illustrates the point. According to the program’s account, he instead wrote instructions for a staffer to deliver orally. If accurate, that is not merely farcical behavior. It is an attempt to preserve pressure while reducing personal exposure.

The scandal is the permission system

AlterNet’s catalogue risks making corruption look like a collection of individual appetites: an enormous consulting contract, a donor asked to cover a credit-card bill, political work abroad, campaign operatives enriching themselves. But the connective tissue is institutional.

The relevant question is who can authorize access, contracts, pardons, appointments and campaign money—and who can punish insiders for taking too much without permission. Last’s claim that the “cardinal sin” is failing to make Trump whole is commentary, not a proven rule. Still, the reported intervention in the Habba Mildon contract supports a narrower conclusion: the arrangement became unacceptable when Trump objected, not when the conflict described by the Times allegedly arose.

The weaker actors are not the center

A story framed as “all the grifting” encourages readers to focus on disposable courtiers. That misdirects attention from the office that gives their services value. Kimberly Guilfoyle’s alleged request, Parscale’s reported earnings and the other episodes matter, but none explains the system without the political authority surrounding them.

The lesser figures retain agency. They allegedly sought money, arranged deals or sold political services. But treating them as the primary cause mistakes vendors for the market-maker. The president, senior officials and campaign leadership possess the power to set boundaries, enforce ethics rules and deny access. When those boundaries depend on personal favor, enforcement becomes selective by design, whatever any participant’s private motive.

Government as a private franchise

The larger pattern is patrimonial politics: public authority administered as though it were the leader’s personal franchise. Loyalty determines access. Permission substitutes for rules. Insiders compete to monetize proximity, then discover that proximity belongs to the person at the center.

That system does not need every allegation in AlterNet’s compilation to be proven in order to reveal its political danger. The reporting’s strongest evidence is structural: a pardon seeker’s family allegedly entered a vast contract with a Justice Department official, and the president reportedly intervened over the payment. The essential failure is not that Trumpworld contains opportunists. It is that public power appears to function as the commodity around which their opportunities are built.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.
